This meeting will be conducted in a hybrid model with both in-person and virtual attendance. Attend this meeting
remotely using Zoom. To request to speak, use the “raise hand” function in Zoom. To join by phone: Dial 1-669-
254-5252 or 1-833-568-8864 (Toll Free) and enter Meeting ID: 165 636 2224. To provide public comment, Press
*9 and wait to be recognized by the Chair. To submit a written communication for the public record, email
council@berkeleyca.gov.

Live captioned broadcasts of Council meetings are available on B-TV (Channel 33) and via internet video stream.
All Council meetings are recorded.

This meeting will be conducted in accordance with the Brown Act, Government Code Section 54953. Any member
of the public may attend this meeting, however, if you are feeling sick, please do not attend the meeting in person.
The City Council may take action related to any subject listed on the Agenda.

Pursuant to the City Council Rules of Procedure and State Law, the presiding officer may remove, or cause the
removal of, an individual for disrupting the meeting. Prior to removing an individual, the presiding officer shall
warn the individual that their behavior is disrupting the meeting and that their failure to cease their behavior may
result in their removal. The presiding officer may then remove the individual if they do not promptly cease their
disruptive behavior. “Disrupting” means engaging in behavior during a meeting of a legislative body that actually
disrupts, disturbs, impedes, or renders infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting and includes, but is not
limited to, a failure to comply with reasonable and lawful regulations adopted by a legislative body, or engaging in
behavior that constitutes use of force or a true threat of force.

Government Code Section 84308 (Levine Act) - Parties to a proceeding involving a license, permit, or other
entitlement for use are required to disclose if they made contributions over $500 within the prior 12 months to any
City employee or officer. Parties and participants with a financial interest are prohibited from making more than
$500 in contributions to a decisionmaker for the 12 months after the final decision is rendered on the proceeding.
The above contribution disclosures and restrictions do not apply when the proceeding is competitively bid, or
involves a personnel or labor contract. For more information, see Government Code Section 84308.

Preliminary Matters
 Roll Call:

 Land Acknowledgement Statement: The City of Berkeley recognizes that the community we
 live in was built on the territory of xučyun (Huchiun (Hooch-yoon)), the ancestral and unceded land of the
 Chochenyo (Cho-chen-yo)-speaking Ohlone (Oh-low-nee) people, the ancestors and descendants of the
 sovereign Verona Band of Alameda County. This land was and continues to be of great importance to all
 of the Ohlone Tribes and descendants of the Verona Band. As we begin our meeting tonight, we
 acknowledge and honor the original inhabitants of Berkeley, the documented 5,000-year history of a
 vibrant community at the West Berkeley Shellmound, and the Ohlone people who continue to reside in
 the East Bay. We recognize that Berkeley’s residents have and continue to benefit from the use and
 occupation of this unceded stolen land since the City of Berkeley’s incorporation in 1878. As stewards of
 the laws regulating the City of Berkeley, it is not only vital that we recognize the history of this land, but
 also recognize that the Ohlone people are present members of Berkeley and other East Bay communities
 today. The City of Berkeley will continue to build relationships with the Lisjan Tribe and to create
 meaningful actions that uphold the intention of this land acknowledgement.

 Ceremonial Matters: In addition to those items listed on the agenda, the Mayor may add additional
 ceremonial matters.

 City Manager Comments: The City Manager may make announcements or provide information to
 the City Council in the form of an oral report. The Council will not take action on such items but may
 request the City Manager place a report on a future agenda for discussion.

 Public Comment on Non-Agenda Matters: Up to ten persons will be selected to address
 matters not on the Council agenda. If five or fewer persons are identified to provide non-agenda
 comment, each person selected will be allotted two minutes each. If more than five persons are selected
 to address matters not on the Council agenda, each person selected will be allotted one minute each.
 In-person attendees wishing to address the Council on matters not on the Council agenda during the
 initial ten-minute period for such comment, must submit a speaker card to the City Clerk in person at the
 meeting location and prior to the moment that the Presiding Officer calls for public comment on non-
 agenda items. Remote attendees must raise their hand in the videoconference application when the
 Presiding Officer calls for non-agenda speakers. The first five raised hands on the videoconference
 application will be selected to speak and the first five cards drawn at the meeting will be selected to
 speak. The number of in-person and remote speakers selected may be adjusted by the Presiding Officer
 if fewer than five speakers from either format are identified.

 The remainder of the speakers wishing to address the Council on non-agenda items will be heard at the
 end of the agenda.

 Public Comment by Employee Unions (first regular meeting of the month): This
 period of public comment is reserved for officially designated representatives of City of Berkeley
 employee unions, with five minutes allocated per union if representatives of three or fewer unions wish to
 speak and up to three minutes per union if representatives of four or more unions wish to speak.

 Consent Calendar
     The Council will first determine whether to move items on the agenda for “Action” or “Information” to the
     “Consent Calendar”, or move “Consent Calendar” items to “Action.” Three members of the City Council
     must agree to pull an item from the Consent Calendar or Information Calendar for it to move to Action.
     Items that remain on the “Consent Calendar” are voted on in one motion as a group. “Information” items
     are not discussed or acted upon at the Council meeting unless they are moved to “Action” or “Consent”.
     No additional items can be moved onto the Consent Calendar once public comment has commenced. At
     any time during, or immediately after, public comment on Information and Consent items, any
     Councilmember may move any Information or Consent item to “Action.” Following this, the Council will
     vote on the items remaining on the Consent Calendar in one motion.
     For items moved to the Action Calendar from the Consent Calendar or Information Calendar, persons
     who spoke on the item during the Consent Calendar public comment period may speak again at the time
     the matter is taken up during the Action Calendar.

     Public Comment on Consent Calendar and Information Items Only: The Council will
     take public comment on any items that are either on the amended Consent Calendar or the Information
     Calendar. If ten or fewer persons are interested in speaking on an individual agenda item, each speaker
     may speak for two minutes. If there are more than ten persons interested in speaking, the Presiding
     Officer may limit the public comment for all speakers to one minute per speaker. Speakers are permitted
     to yield their time to one other speaker, however no one speaker shall have more than four minutes. The
     Presiding Officer may, with the consent of persons representing both sides of an issue, allocate a block of
     time to each side to present their issue. A speaker may only speak once during the period for public
     comment on Consent Calendar and Information items.

     Additional information regarding public comment by City of Berkeley employees and interns: Employees
     and interns of the City of Berkeley, although not required, are encouraged to identify themselves as such,
     the department in which they work and state whether they are speaking as an individual or in their official
     capacity when addressing the Council in open session or workshops.

25.   Amendment to Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 7.18 to Explicitly Require
      Competitive Procurement for Services to Promote Accountability and
      Transparency and Refer Development of Regulations to City Manager
      (Reviewed by the Budget & Finance Committee)
      From: Councilmember Kesarwani (Author), Mayor Ishii (Co-Sponsor),
      Councilmember Taplin (Co-Sponsor), Councilmember Bartlett (Co-Sponsor)
      Recommendation: Adopt an ordinance amending Berkeley Municipal Code (BMC)
      Chapter 7.18, Expenditure Limitations, to require procurement through competitive
      solicitation for all city contracts for professional services and other services greater
      than $100,000.
      Further, for the City Attorney’s Office (CAO), require development of an Outside
      Council Selection Protocol whereby the CAO develops an annual report to Council
      for its pre-qualified list of outside attorneys and law firms based on respondents to
      the office’s ongoing Request for Qualifications process. When outside counsel is
      required, senior staff in the CAO would choose from pre-qualified attorneys/firms and
      identify the best candidate based on expertise, quality of work, and cost. This
      recommendation would allow for a competitive process using the pre-qualified list,
      thus accommodating the CAO’s need to quickly engage outside counsel while
      preserving best procurement practices. Additionally, request the CAO report to
      Council on legal services contracts and amendments to City Council quarterly to
      increase transparency of spending on legal services contracts.
      Refer to the City Manager to promulgate any further regulations that may be needed
      related to the requirement for competitive solicitation except for emergencies and
      when market research justifies the business case for a sole-source procurement, in
      alignment with the existing purchasing manual. Further, refer to the CAO to develop
      legal services regulations to implement the competitive solicitation process for
      outside counsel contracts and define circumstances where a sole-source
      procurement is justified by emergencies, market research, conflicts of interest, or
      other considerations.
      Policy Committee Recommendation: To send the item to Council with a Qualified
      Positive Recommendation as written and amended during discussion, with additional
      direction to further consider:
      -Specifying the 5-7 year contract rebidding timeframe in the ordinance as well as the
      purchasing manual
      -Authorizing the City Attorney’s Office to promulgate legal services procurement
      regulations and guidelines
      -Establishing annual reporting to Council on legal services contracts and
      amendments
      -B.M.C. Section 7.18.010(A) Expenditures pursuant to Charter Article XI, Sections 67
      and 67.5 is amended to read as follows:
      Except as otherwise provided in this Title, expenditures pursuant to Article XI,
      Sections 67 and 67.5 of the Charter of the City of Berkeley, for which exceed the
      initial amount exceeds of $1050,000, inclusive only of professional services, other
      services, supplies, equipment, or materials (excluding leases and real estate
      agreements), shall require Council approval and shall be procured through
      competitive solicitation except in the case of emergencies pursuant to Article XI,
      Section 67.4. The requirement specified in Article XI, Section 67 of the Charter to

Action Calendar
  The public may comment on each item listed on the agenda for action. For items moved to the Action
  Calendar from the Consent Calendar or Information Calendar, persons who spoke on the item during the
  Consent Calendar public comment period may speak again during the Action Calendar public comment
  period on the item
  The Presiding Officer will request that persons wishing to speak line up at the podium, or use the "raise
  hand" function in Zoom, to determine the number of persons interested in speaking at that time. If ten or
  fewer persons are interested in speaking on an individual agenda item, each speaker may speak for two
  minutes. If there are more than ten persons interested in speaking, the Presiding Officer may limit the
  public comment for all speakers to one minute per speaker. Speakers are permitted to yield their time to
  one other speaker, however no one speaker shall have more than four minutes. The Presiding Officer may,
  with the consent of persons representing both sides of an issue, allocate a block of time to each side to
  present their issue.
  Action items may be reordered at the discretion of the Chair with the consent of Council.
  The Presiding Officer may open and close an additional comment period for Action items on this agenda
  (excluding any public hearings, appeals, and/or quasi-judicial matters), at the start of the Action Calendar.
  Those who speak on an item during this comment period may not speak a second time when the item is
  taken up by Council.

  approve or deny a use permit or variance for a project the following requirements and restrictions apply:
  1) No lawsuit challenging a City decision to deny (Code Civ. Proc. §1094.6(b)) or approve (Gov. Code

  Decision of the action of the City Council is mailed. Any lawsuit not filed within that 90-day period will be
  barred. 2) In any lawsuit that may be filed against a City Council decision to approve or deny a use
  permit or variance, the issues and evidence will be limited to those raised by you or someone else, orally
  or in writing, at a public hearing or prior to the close of the last public hearing on the project.

                               ORDINANCE NO. 8,035-N.S.

AMENDMENTS TO TITLE 23 (ZONING ORDINANCE) OF BERKELEY MUNICIPAL
CODE TO REQUIRE UNDERGROUNDING OF TRANSFORMERS ON PRIVATE
PROPERTY

BE IT ORDAINED by the Council of the City of Berkeley as follows:

Section 1. That Berkeley Municipal Code Section 23.304.100 is amended to read as
follows:


23.304.100      Site Features.

A. Residential and Commercial Zoning Districts. The standards in this section apply in
all Residential and Commercial zoning districts, and to all residential, commercial, and
mixed-use projects.

       1. Electrical Distribution Equipment. Electrical Distribution Equipment means
       primary-voltage electrical distribution system equipment, including but not limited
       to transformers, switches and fuses, and junction bars, and associated pads and
       enclosures needed for installation, operation, and maintenance.

       2. Above Grade and Pad-Mounted Electrical Distribution Equipment
       Prohibited: No Electrical Distribution Equipment serving the development shall be
       installed above grade on a private parcel, except where the City Engineer
       determines that it is not in the public interest to site electric distribution equipment
       within the public right-of-way.

       3. Electrical Distribution Equipment within Public Right-of-Way. Approval of
       the placement of any Electrical Distribution Equipment within the public right-of-
       way shall be at the sole discretion of the City Engineer and shall be based on
       protection of public safety, ADA accessibility, pedestrian and bicycle access,
       emergency response, existing and future public infrastructure, streetscape
       impacts, utility conflicts, operations, and maintenance considerations. Nothing in
       this section requires Public Works or the City Engineer to identify, design, or
       approve a location in the public right-of-way.




Ordinance No. 8,035-N.S.                                                        Page 1 of 2
                                                                                     Page 19
                                        Page 2 of 2




B. Residential Districts. The standards in this section apply in Residential Districts.

   1. Garbage Cans. All garbage cans shall be effectively screened from view from the
   public right-of-way and surrounding properties.

   2. Utility Meters. For buildings with two or more units, all utility meters shall be
   effectively screened from view from the public right-of-way and surrounding
   properties.

    3. Pedestrian Walkway for Multiple Dwellings.

        a. All multi-family dwellings shall have an unobstructed walkway for pedestrian
        access from the public right-of-way to the building.

        b. The required walkway shall be separated and physically protected from a
        driveway or off-street parking spaces with a minimum 2-foot wide landscaped strip.

    4. Exterior Lighting.

        a. All exterior lighting shall be shielded and directed downward and away from lot
        lines to prevent excessive glare beyond the property on which the light is located.

        b. Lights on motion sensors may not be triggered by movement or activity located
        off the property on which the light is located.

Section 2. Copies of this Ordinance shall be posted for two days prior to adoption in the
display case located near the walkway in front of the Maudelle Shirek Building, 2134
Martin Luther King Jr. Way. Within 15 days of adoption, copies of this Ordinance shall be
filed at each branch of the Berkeley Public Library and the title shall be published in a
newspaper of general circulation.

City Attorney’s Office
                                                                             CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                             October 27, 2026



To:               Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:             Farimah Brown, City Attorney
                  Nathan Dahl, Assistant to the City Attorney
Subject:          Waiver of Sanctuary City Ordinance for Westlaw Contract

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution waiving the contract prohibition of Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter
13.105, Sanctuary City Contracting, in order to enter into a contract with Westlaw.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
In order to provide legal services, the City Attorney’s Office (“CAO”) relies on external
legal resources. The preeminent provider of legal resources is Westlaw, a Thomsen
Reuters Company. However, Westlaw also provides services to the United States
Immigration and Customs Enforcement Department, among its many customers.
Pursuant to Chapter 13.105, the Sanctuary City Contracting Ordinance, the Council
must grant a waiver in order for the City to contract with Westlaw.

BACKGROUND
The CAO currently has a contract in place with Westlaw, set to expire November 30,
2026. The current contract was approved on June 1, 2021 by Council Resolution #
69,907 and required a waiver of the contract prohibition of Berkeley Municipal Code
Chapter 13.105, the Sanctuary City Contracting Ordinance (“Ordinance”).

One of the most critical tasks performed by attorneys is legal research. From
researching cases and statutes for litigation to preparing ordinances and reviewing
contract terms, having a robust and comprehensive legal research tool is indispensable.
Since 2000 and until the passage of the Ordinance in 2019, the CAO has contracted
with Westlaw, a Thomson Reuters company. Westlaw is relied upon by numerous legal
organizations, governmental agencies, and non-profit organizations.

Current subscribers include entities such as the Federal and California courts,
as well as hundreds of law firms of all sizes. Westlaw is essential to work done by city
attorneys, public defense agencies, legal aid associations and prosecutors. In firms with



    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/
                                                                                                     Page 21
                                                Page 2 of 4



Waiver of Sanctuary City Ordinance for Westlaw Contract                CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026



more than 500 attorneys, Westlaw is the legal resource service of choice for 75% of
those firms and is the leading platform in the legal industry, relied on for:

       Accuracy of case law, statutes and regulations, all of which are interconnected
        through its proprietary Key Number System, a master classification system of
        U.S. law, which organizes legal authorities by topic, enabling researchers to
        readily locate pertinent cases, statutes, regulations and other sources, and track
        the evolution of various legal concepts.
        system.

       Exclusive content critical to municipal attorneys, such as McQuillen: The Law of
        Municipal Corporations, Matthews Municipal Ordinances, and The Ordinance
        Law Annotations.

       In addition to the exclusive and proprietary sources described above, the
        following critical legal research resources are also proprietary to Westlaw:
        California Jurisprudence, the Rutter Group Collection, Miller & Starr CA Real
        Estate, Witkin Library, American Law Reports, CA Civil Practice Collection, CA
        Judges BenchBook Series and CA Code Forms Government1.

The Ordinance, adopted in 2019, prohibits contracting with an entity that provides
services to the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement Department
unless a waiver is granted by the Council. Section 13.105.030 provides that a waiver
can be granted “…based on a specific determination that no reasonable alternative
exists, taking into consideration the following:

1. The intent and purpose of this ordinance;
2. The availability of alternative services, goods and equipment; and
3. Quantifiable additional costs resulting from use of available alternatives.”

The intent and purpose of the Ordinance is to ensure that the City does not financially
support any company that provides services that infringe upon the rights of immigrants.
Here, the CAO will be using Westlaw to, among other things, enhance efforts to protect
immigrant rights as needed.

With respect to availability of alternative services, as explained above, due to the
specialized and proprietary nature of Westlaw services, no alternative exists to provide
the level of resources offered by Westlaw. Additionally, the second most used legal
research software with 14% of the market – LexisNexis – also provides data services to
the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement Department. Not only is
LexisNexis also not in compliance with the Sanctuary City Contracting Ordinance, its
software also lacks the capability of Westlaw’s products. Consequently, no additional
costs have been identified for an alternative service provider which can provide services
equivalent to those offered by Westlaw as not comparable alternative exists.



                                                    Page 2
                                                                                  Page 22
                                                Page 3 of 4



Waiver of Sanctuary City Ordinance for Westlaw Contract                 CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                            October 27, 2026




ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
While much of the proprietary publications identified above were previously only
available in print (and are still available in print today), the CAO intends to contract only
for online access to these sources, thereby significantly reducing reliance on print
publications and the concomitant negative impact on the environment.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The CAO requires services provided by Westlaw and no comparable alternative exists.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
None.

                             RESOLUTION NO. ##,###-N.S.

ADOPT A RESOLUTION WAIVING THE CONTRACT REQUIREMENTS OF THE
SANCTUARY CITY CONTRACTING ORDINANCE PURSUANT TO CHAPTER 13.105
OF THE BERKELEY MUNICIPAL CODE, IN ORDER TO ENTER INTO A CONTRACT
WITH WESTLAW, A THOMSON REUTERS COMPANY

WHEREAS, Pursuant to Ordinance No. 7650-N.S. and Chapter 13.105, the Sanctuary
City Contracting Ordinance (“Ordinance”), in order to enter into a contract with Westlaw,
a Thomson Reuters Company, the City Council must determine that no reasonable
alternative exists based on consideration of three factors; and

WHEREAS, the three factors identified in the Ordinance ((1) The intent and purpose of
the Ordinance, (2) the availability of alternative service providers, and (3) quantifiable
additional costs resulting from the use of alternative providers) have all been
considered; and

WHEREAS, the use of services provided by Westlaw is indispensable to the practice of
law; and

WHEREAS, contracting with Westlaw will not violate the intent of the Ordinance as its
services will be used to promote the interest of the immigrant community in
conformance with the intent and purpose of the Ordinance; and

WHEREAS, no other contractors are available who can provide comparable services
required by this contract; and

WHEREAS, no additional costs are quantifiable as there are no available alternatives;
and

WHEREAS, failing to provide this waiver would result in additional costs to use Westlaw
on an a la carte basis.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Berkeley that a
waiver to the "no-contract" provision of the B.M.C. Section 13.105 is approved because
no reasonable alternative exists to the services that will be provided under contract with
Westlaw, a Thomsen Reuters Company.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Each of the City commissions that were active during the reporting period submitted an
annual attendance report covering the period of September 1, 2025 through August 31,
2026 (Attachment 1). These reports include the number of meetings, meeting
cancellations, commissioners in attendance, length of meetings, number of speakers, and
members of the public present. The reports also reflect the number of vacant positions
on the commission as of August 31, 2026. Attachment 2 provides a summary of the
approved leaves of absence for each commission.

Resolution No. 72,097-N.S. establishes the meeting frequency for all commissions in
accordance with current state law and City policy. Consistent with Resolution No. 72,097-
N.S., commissions are divided into four categories (A, B, C, and D) depending on whether
they have time-sensitive, legally mandated business to complete. The meeting activity for
the reporting period of September 1, 2025 through August 31, 2026, has been broken
down by category below.

Upon review of the meeting reports, the City Council may recommend that commissions
be reorganized, or reclassified into a different meeting frequency category. Commissions
that do not demonstrate a significant level of activity and engagement may be placed in
the six-meeting-per-year category.

BACKGROUND
On June 14, 2005, the City Council discussed the reduction of commission meetings as
a cost-saving measure, and adopted a proposal which created three categories of
commission meeting schedules, a process for requesting Council approval of any extra
meetings, direction to commission secretaries to submit an information report whenever
a commission cancels two consecutive meetings for lack of quorum, and an annual
attendance report.

On January 15, 2008, Council adopted Resolution No. 63,949–N.S., which updated the
commission meeting frequency schedule to include a fourth category of meeting
frequency.

On March 17, 2020, the council adopted Resolution No. 69,331–N.S. with the purpose of
reducing the number of commission meeting schedules from four categories to two
categories. This decision was made in response to the mandatory Shelter-in-Place order
imposed as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

On November 28, 2023, the council adopted Resolution No. 71,109-N.S. restoring the
meeting frequency categories to their previous count of four categories, as initially
adopted by the council prior to the pandemic.

On January 27, 2026, the Council adopted Resolution No. 72,097-N.S., which
incorporated the Safe Streets Citizen Oversight Committee into the City’s commission
meeting frequency schedule.

There are no identifiable environmental effects, climate impacts, or sustainability
opportunities associated with the subject of this report.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The annual commission attendance report informs the Council of commission activity
and allows for comparison with the meeting frequency schedule. The annual attendance
report documents increased demand on or under-utilization of commissions and allows
Council to make changes to the meeting frequency schedule accordingly.

                                                                             October 27, 2026

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Carianna Arredondo, Assistant to the City Manager
Subject:         Contract: Adrien Segal Public Artwork Commission for Santa Fe Trackbed to
                 Park Conversion

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute a contract and any
necessary amendments with Adrien Segal for an amount not to exceed $150,000 for a
public art commission of two unique vertical structures that will serve as habitat boxes
for both birds and insects at the Community Garden Park (between Blake and Parker
Streets) and the Urban Farm and Education Park (between Derby and Ward Streets).

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The $150,000 contract will be funded through the Cultural Trust Fund 148-21-211-000-
0000-000-446-612990- in Fiscal Year 2027. Funds will be requested to be appropriated
during the Annual Appropriations Ordinance process.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Artist Adrien Segal was selected through a competitive process to create two distinct
artworks—one artwork installed at each site -- Community Garden Park (between Blake
and Parker Streets) and the Urban Farm and Education Park (between Derby and Ward
Streets). Each structure must stand vertically for high visibility to park visitors and
function effectively as both a bird and insect habitat. Artworks will be installed
permanently and must be structurally sound, highly durable, and easy to maintain. The
goals of the project are:

      1. Create permanent structures that effectively offer shelter and nesting
         opportunities for native and migratory birds, as well as non-stinging insects.
         Structures will be made of highly durable materials, and their design considers
         safety, maintenance, weatherization, and vandalism.

      2. Integrate strong design aesthetics with a focus on environmental awareness and
         park integration. Artworks will be appropriate for the site in terms of scale,
         medium, design, and imagery, and will complement the context of the
         surrounding area.

    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/

    3. Develop bold, visually striking installations at both ends of the park corridor to
       serve as key points of interest.

Adrien Segal’s proposal Murmur Nest is inspired by the motion and flight of birds and
insects as they skillfully navigate the sky. These visually striking 9’ tall 3D printed wood
adobe sculptures will serve as bold visual landmarks at each end of the park.
Integrating layered textures, swooping curvature, and micro-alcoves, they will offer
cavity nesting habitat and sheltered perches for birds and non-stinging insects as they
seek rest and shelter on their pollination and migratory journey across Berkeley. (Figure
1.)




Figure 1: Artwork proposal by Adrian Segal, Murmur Nest, 3D printed adobe for Santa Fe Trackbed to Park
Conversion (2027).

Staff anticipate that the two artworks will be installed by late September 2027.

BACKGROUND
The Santa Fe 1 to Park Conversion project will transform four blocks of former railroad
property between Blake and Ward Streets, crossing Acton Street, into new
neighborhood parkland. The City acquired the railroad property in 1980 and
subsequently converted portions of the corridor into parks, pathways, housing, and


1 https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/our-work/capital-projects/santa-fe-trackbed-park-conversion




                                                     Page 2
                                                                                                      Page 64
                                                   Page 3 of 7


Contract: Adrien Segal Public Artwork Commission                      CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




community gardens. This project continues that effort by developing some of the
remaining undeveloped parcels in South Berkeley.

In 2021, the City received a $5 million Proposition 68 Statewide Parks Program grant to
support the conversion. Additional funding from Measure T1 and Parks Tax funds
supports completion of the project. Informed by community input, the park design
includes a community garden, dog park, outdoor exercise stations, a playground with a
tot cycle track, and an outdoor classroom with a teaching garden and orchard. The
project includes soil remediation followed by park construction, expanding access to
green space and outdoor recreation.

The public art commission will complement these recreational and educational
amenities by integrating sculptural habitat structures into two park sites. The artworks
are intended to create distinctive focal points, provide shelter and nesting opportunities
for birds and insects, and encourage visitors to engage with the surrounding
environment.

On February 26, 2025, the Civic Arts Commission approved the Santa Fe Trackbed to
Park Conversion Public Art Project Plan, which called for the commission of two unique
vertical structures that will serve as habitat boxes for both birds and insects at the
Community Garden Park (between Blake and Parker Streets) and the Urban Farm and
Education Park (between Derby and Ward Streets) as follows: M/S/C (Woo/Pineda) to
approve Public Art Project Plan for the Santa Fe Trackbed to Park Conversion Vote:
Ayes — Bachrach, Blecher, Bullwinkel, Covarrubias, Pineda, Scott, Woo; Nays —
None; Abstain — None.

A Request for Qualifications for this public art commission was released on November
13, 2025, and was open through January 12, 2026 (Specification No. 25-11729-C). A
selection panel comprised of 8 arts professionals and subject matter experts reviewed
the qualifications of the 72 applicants and recommended 14 applications to be
presented to the Santa Fe Trackbed to Park Conversion selection panel. The selection
panel was comprised of three Bay Area arts professionals, a Civic Arts Commissioner, a
Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commissioner, a member of the building’s
architecture team, an entomologist, and an ornithologist. This panel reviewed the
qualifications of the 14 recommended artists and advanced 3 finalists to develop
detailed conceptual site-specific proposals.

Once the 3 finalist proposals were received, staff conducted extensive community
outreach to collect public input on the proposals. A “Berkeley Considers” survey was
hosted on the City’s website from August 6 to August 24, 2026, inviting public for input
on each proposal and at the close of the survey, 695 responses were collected and
reviewed by the panel equaling 34.75 hours of public comment.

On August 31, 2026, the selection panel was reconvened to consider finalists’
presentations in an interview format. At the end of three rounds of competitive scoring,
the selection panel recommended Adrien Segal’s proposal Murmur Nest to the Public
Art Subcommittee for approval.

On September 3, 2026, the Public Art Subcommittee unanimously recommended
Adrien Segal’s proposal Murmur Nest to the Civic Arts Commission for approval.

On September 22, 2026, the Civic Arts Commission unanimously approved Adrien
Segal’s proposal Murmur Nest with the following vote: M/S/C (Dutta-Choudhury
/Pineda) to approve Public Art Project Plan for the Santa Fe Trackbed to Park
Conversion Vote: Ayes — Bachrach, Blecher, Dutta-Choudhury, Montgomery, Pineda,
Woo; Nays — None; Abstain — None; Absent — Bullwinkel (LoA), Kramer (LoA), Scott

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The proposed artworks, including their foundations and installation, are within the scope
of the Santa Fe Trackbed to Park Conversion project covered by the City’s July 2021
Notice of Exemption under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Installation
will involve localized foundation work, material deliveries, and temporary use of
construction equipment. Associated noise, dust, vehicle emissions, and soil disturbance
are within the scope of the park project’s environmental determination, and no additional
CEQA review is required. Installation will be coordinated with park construction.

The artworks are designed to provide shelter and nesting opportunities for birds and
non-stinging insects. The proposed wood adobe combines salvaged redwood fiber,
water, clay, and a cellulose binder, incorporating reclaimed material into the sculptures.
They will also encourage public awareness of local wildlife and urban habitat.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
 Adrien Segal’s proposal, Murmur Nest, was selected through a competitive process
using the criteria published in the RFQ: creativity, experience, project goals, site
specificity, feasibility and maintenance, and project management. These criteria align
with the City’s public art approval considerations concerning originality, artist
qualifications, relevance to the site, feasibility, and long-term maintenance, and
complies with the process outlined with BMC 6.14.010 “Visual Art in Public Places.”

The proposed sculptures respond to the park’s natural environment and educational
purpose by combining public art with habitat for birds and non-stinging insects. Their
distinctive design will enhance the two park sites-- the Community Garden Park
(between Blake and Parker Streets) and the Urban Farm and Education Park (between
Derby and Ward Streets)-- and provide opportunities for community engagement with
art and local ecology. Public input informed the selection panel’s review, and the
proposal received unanimous recommendations from the Public Art Subcommittee and
approval by the Civic Arts Commission

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
None. The City Council could defer or decline authorization of the contract. Deferral
could delay fabrication and installation of the artworks. Declining authorization would
require staff to reassess the public art commission and return with an alternative
approach. Staff recommends proceeding with the selected proposal based on the
competitive selection process and its alignment with the project’s goals.

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to amend Contract No. 32500002 with
Community Initiatives | Live Free USA for gun violence intervention and prevention
services to add $257,548 in Byrne State Crisis Intervention Program (SCIP) grant
funding pursuant to a budget modification approved by the California Board of State and
Community Corrections (BSCC), bringing the total contract not-to-exceed amount to
$2,874,768; extend the contract term through December 31, 2027; and update the
scope of services and budget accordingly.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The proposed amendment incorporates an additional $257,548 in SCIP funding into the
contract through a BSCC-approved budget modification. These funds are being
reallocated within the City’s existing grant award and do not increase the total award or
require additional General Fund support. The revised contract not-to-exceed amount of
$2,874,768 includes the original contract funding, previously authorized SCIP funding,
the previously approved $200,000 General Fund allocation, and the additional SCIP
funding requested through this action. The General Fund allocation were awarded
through the Mayor’s final Budget Recommendations and will be appropriated as part of
the Annual Appropriations Ordinance.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The City’s Gun Violence Intervention and Prevention Program (GVIPP) coordinates
community-based outreach, violence interruption, and supportive services for
individuals at elevated risk of firearm-related harm. Community Initiatives | Live Free
USA serves as the City’s community-based violence intervention partner, providing
trauma-informed engagement, life coaching, case management, crisis stabilization, and
referrals to services.

During SCIP implementation, the City identified $210,044 in Crime Analyst personnel
savings and $47,504 in available technology funding within the original grant allocation.
The Berkeley Police Department (BPD) supports redirecting these resources to
strengthen Live Free USA’s community-based services. BSCC approved the City’s
request to reallocate the combined $257,548 for this purpose.

The proposed amendment incorporates these funds into the contract, updates the
scope and budget, and extends the term through December 31, 2027. The amended
scope supports proactive outreach, individualized service planning, ongoing participant
engagement, and crisis stabilization following shooting incidents or credible threats of
retaliation.

GVIPP advances the Strategic Plan goal to create a resilient, safe, connected, and
prepared city.

Effective January 1, 2026, local agencies are required to satisfy noticing requirements
for certain contracts for services that meet the criteria outlined in Government Code
Section 3504.1 as amended by AB 339. This project does not meet the criteria in
Government Code Section 3504.1 and is exempt from the noticing requirement.

BACKGROUND
GVIPP builds on the City’s Reimagining Public Safety initiative and the 2023 Gun
Violence Prevention Report, combining community-based intervention with law
enforcement coordination.

The City entered into Contract No. 32500002 with Community Initiatives | Live Free
USA on July 1, 2024, with an original not-to-exceed amount of $2,000,000, to support
program implementation.

The City subsequently received a $1 million SCIP award to support Crime Analyst
staffing, expanded Live Free USA services, and investigative technology. On July 29,
2025, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 71,907-N.S., authorizing acceptance of
the award and related actions, including amendment of the Live Free USA contract. The
grant allocation included $417,220 for Live Free USA services.




                                              Page 2
                                                                                        Page 72
                                           Page 3 of 6

Contract No. 32500002 Amendment: Community Initiatives | Live Free USA for
Gun Violence Intervention and Prevention Services                            CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                                 October 27, 2026




In its June 9, 2026 report, Live Free reported reaching 56 individuals, maintaining 26
active participants, and completing 28 gun violence-related mediations. Eleven
participants obtained employment, including 10 who remained employed; six secured
stable housing; and 18 connected with additional programs and services. All five youth
participants demonstrated educational progress, and three graduated from high school.
Berkeley also recorded zero gun violence-related homicides or injuries in 2025,
alongside GVIPP implementation and broader City public safety efforts. The June report
highlighted NICJR’s Cost of Gun Violence in Berkeley analysis, which estimated
taxpayer costs of approximately $3.2 million per fatal shooting and $726,000 per
nonfatal injury shooting. Applied to the shootings reported in 2024, these estimates total
approximately $13.3 million across local, county, and state systems, underscoring the
human and fiscal importance of prevention.

During the FY2027–FY2028 budget process, Mayor Adena Ishii recommended
$200,000 in General Fund support for Live Free USA. The City Council incorporated
this allocation into the biennial budget through Resolution No. 72,340-N.S., adopted
June 23, 2026.

The proposed amendment builds on these prior funding commitments by incorporating
the additional $257,548 in SCIP funding approved through the budget modification
described above. The revised total contract amount includes the previously approved
General Fund allocation and $674,768 in combined SCIP funding. The additional
resources and extension through December 31, 2027 will support continued outreach,
mediation, and life coaching, with anticipated outcomes of sustained participant
engagement, reduced retaliation risk, and improved employment, housing, and
educational stability.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
No direct environmental sustainability or climate impacts are anticipated from this
contract amendment.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The proposed amendment aligns the contract amount, scope, and term with the
additional funding identified for GVIPP implementation. It implements the City Council’s
$200,000 General Fund allocation and incorporates $257,548 in SCIP Grant resources
into the service agreement. Continuing services through the existing contractor supports
established participant relationships and coordination with City and community partners.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The City Council could decline the proposed amendment. Staff would then need to
assess adjustments to service levels and duration and coordinate with BSCC regarding
an alternative use of the reallocated SCIP funds.

To:                   Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:                 Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by:         David Sprague, Fire Chief
Subject:              Contract: Insight Public Sector, Inc. dba Aurelian for non-emergency call-
                      taking software

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager or their designee to enter into a
“piggyback” contract with Insight Public Sector, Inc. dba Aurelian for non-emergency call
taking software for the Emergency Communications Center and services using the
cooperative purchasing organization Omnia Partners Contract No. 23-6692-03. The
contract base period will begin on December 1, 2026, through April 30, 2028, and will
not exceed $197,642.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The total cost, covering the period from December 1, 2026, through April 30, 2028, will
not exceed $197,642. All funds required to pay for this contract will be paid for by
Measure FF (Fire & Emergency Services, 2020).

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The Emergency Communications Center handles approximately 196,000 incoming and
outgoing police and fire calls annually. Only about one-quarter of this telephone
workload consists of incoming 911 calls; the remainder includes calls received through
the City’s non-emergency and administrative lines, as well as outgoing calls made by
dispatch staff in the course of their work. This is consistent with the City Auditor’s 2019
Dispatch Workload report (911 Dispatchers: Understaffing Leads to Excessive Overtime
and Low Morale), which found that total telephone activity increased from approximately
184,000 calls in 2013 to more than 256,000 in 2017, including 55,587 911 calls, and
concluded that “the majority of this increase came from a rise in non-emergency calls
into the Center and outbound calls.” Current data continue to show that most of the
Center’s telephone workload occurs outside of incoming 911 calls.

The Fire Department seeks to improve how non-emergency and administrative calls are
processed. Aurelian products analyze non-emergency calls in real time and transfers
them instantly when an emergency is detected. It also captures caller details, location,
incident type, and key statements to help dispatchers process the call. This creates a

warm handoff, saves time, eliminates duplicative questions, and moves critical
information to the right place faster.

This item is consistent with the City Strategic Plan goals to “create a resilient, safe,
connected, and prepared city,” to “be a customer-focused organization that provides
excellent, timely, easily accessible service and information,” and to “attract and retain a
talented and diverse City government workforce.”

BACKGROUND
Responsibility for dispatch modernization was assigned to the Fire Department through
the Reimagining Public Safety initiative. The Dispatch Needs Assessment prepared by
Federal Engineering, Inc., was presented to the Public Safety Policy Committee on May
15, 2023, and provided to the full Council on October 29, 2024 (Appendix J)1. The
subsequent analysis by Mission Critical Partners, LLC was also provided to Council on
October 29, 2024 (Appendix J). Each identified that call-handling modernization is
necessary to improve consistency and reduce attrition. To this end, the non-emergency
call taking software offered by Aurelian reduces the number of non-emergency and
administrative calls, reducing overall call volume, so dispatchers can focus on 911 calls.

Aurelian’s non-emergency call taking software consists of two components:

  • The software solution can answer the City’s ten-digit non-emergency phone lines,
    route misdirected callers to the correct department, text relevant resources, monitor
    every call for indications of an emergency and transfer those callers immediately to
    a live telecommunicator, and collect information from routine reports to prepare a
    call for service. The software also supports the languages spoken in the Berkeley
    community.

  • The proposed solution also provides real-time assistive support on handling
    emergency calls detected from the non-emergency phone tree. The system starts
    documenting key information for a warm handoff from the phone tree to the
    dispatcher.

The City is utilizing Omnia Partners contract and procurement process for the Request
for Proposals, following the standard public procurement. The Cobb County Department
of Procurement issued RFP 23-6692 on August 26, 2022. On October 13, 2022, the
Department received 17 proposals. A committee evaluated the proposals using the
criteria established in the RFP; the committee elected to enter into negotiations and
contract with five firms, including Insight Public Sector, a firm that manages contract and
RFP services for Aurelian. The contract term is for 60 months and runs from May 1,
2023 through April 30, 2028.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
This administrative action to purchase dispatch software has no direct environmental or
climate impacts. The project supports efficient deployment of emergency resources,
which may indirectly reduce unnecessary vehicle responses and emissions.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Aurelian provides a tested call-handling solution that can reduce the volume of non-
emergency and administrative calls requiring direct dispatcher attention, creating
additional capacity for Emergency Communications Center staff to complete training
and implement standardized call-processing protocols. This approach is consistent with
the modernization work previously identified through the City’s Reimagining Public
Safety initiative. Both the Federal Engineering, Inc. Dispatch Needs Assessment, and
the subsequent Mission Critical Partners analysis identified call-handling modernization
as necessary to improve consistency and reduce attrition. The proposed Aurelian
implementation, together with the previously approved ProQA protocol dispatch system,
advances those consultant recommendations by reducing avoidable call-handling
workload while standardizing the processing of emergency calls.

Staff recommends procuring the Aurelian system through the OMNIA Partners
cooperative purchasing agreement rather than conducting a separate City solicitation.
The cooperative contract was established through a competitively solicited public
procurement process and allows the City to leverage previously negotiated pricing and
contract terms while avoiding the additional time and administrative expense of
conducting a duplicative request for proposals. Using the cooperative agreement will
allow implementation to proceed more quickly while retaining the benefits of a
competitive procurement process.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The City could choose not to implement a call-screening tool and continue current
dispatch practices. Under this alternative, the Emergency Communications Center
would continue to receive thousands of non-emergency and administrative calls each
month that require attention from professional Telecommunicator staff, reducing the
time available for 911 call handling, training, protocol implementation, and other
modernization work.

The City could also conduct a separate competitive solicitation for a call-screening
solution. Staff does not recommend this approach because it would delay
implementation during a critical period of forward progress in the Emergency
Communications Center, including implementation of other consultant-recommended
operational and call-processing improvements. Agencies using virtual call-handling tools
such as Aurelian or similar products have reported substantial reductions in the volume
of administrative and non-emergency calls reaching 911 call takers.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
This service provides a safety net for consumers when the Mental Health Division’s
Adult Mental Health Clinic experiences a shortage of staff allowed to prescribe
medication. This contract will allow intermittent usage of locum tenens medication
services through Jackson & Coker Locum Tenens, LLC to ensure clients have access to
medication. Locum tenens are licensed and qualified Psychiatrists or Psychiatric Nurse
Practitioners who have a temporary placement at the contracting facility.

A new Request for Proposals (RFP) for locum tenens psychiatry services will be
processed during the second quarter of FY 2027. City Council previously approved
Resolution No. 72,032-N.S., which laid out a plan to complete an RFP before the end of
FY 2026, however, due to subsequent noticing requirements outlined in Government
Code Section 3504.1 as amended by AB 339 involved detailed discussions with labor
unions which did not conclude until June 2026. The current objective is to amend this
contract to provide necessary services throughout the RFP process.

Effective January 1, 2026, local agencies are required to satisfy noticing requirements
for certain contracts for services that meet the criteria outlined in Government Code
Section 3504.1 as amended by AB 339. This project does not meet the criteria in
Government Code Section 3504.1 and is exempt from the noticing requirement.

BACKGROUND
The Mental Health Division has experienced great difficulty in filling vacant positions for
staff who can prescribe psychiatric medications. Due to a variety of factors, including
the Medi-Cal expansion through the Affordable Care Act, an existing shortage of
psychiatrists in the region has been greatly exacerbated. By contracting with a locum
tenens, the City is able to provide constant services when there is staffing turnover, long
term vacancies or additional short-term staffing needs.

Hourly rates for locum tenens psychiatrists and psychiatric nurse practitioners have
increased significantly in recent years, due to the staffing shortages throughout the
region. This contract ensures the City will provide quality mental health care when there
are staffing vacancies. The clear desire is to have career staff working in the clinic, but
locum tenens capacity is needed to continue to serve our clients with medication during
potential vacancies. This contract will provide sufficient funds to ensure that there will
be no interruption in medication services.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
There are no identifiable environmental effects, climate impacts, or sustainability
opportunities associated with the subject of this report.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Jackson & Coker offers locum tenens that provide psychiatric prescriber services to
Medi-Cal, uninsured, disenfranchised, and underserved populations. These services are
necessary for the provision of behavioral health treatment provided by the City. These
services will only be utilized during staff shortages and are not a replacement of
permanent staffing.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The City is required to provide necessary medication prescription and monitoring
services for individuals with mental illness. A shorter contract period and a smaller
amount of funding were considered, but this would require the Mental Health Division to
return with more frequent amendments to this contract over time.

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Scott Ferris, Director, Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront
Subject:         Grant Application: The 2026 Surrendered and Abandoned Vessel Exchange
                 (SAVE) grant program of the California Division of Boating & Waterways

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager or his designee to 1) Submit a grant
application to the California Division of Boating and Waterways (DBW) 2025
Surrendered and Abandoned Vessel Exchange (SAVE) grant program for the removal
and disposal of anticipated abandoned vessels located at the Berkeley Marina; 2)
Accept the grant; 3) Execute any amendments; and 4) Authorize a local match
contribution of $5,000.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The cost to remove and dispose of abandoned and derelict vessels at the Berkeley
Marina through FY2026 is estimated at $95,000. The Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront
Department submitted a grant application to the DBW 2026 SAVE grant program in the
amount of $95,000 for this work. The awarded amount is $50,000, and a local match of
$5,000 (10% of award) is required. Funding for the local match will be recommended for
appropriation through the second amendment to the appropriation ordinance in the
Marina Fund (608). The grant funds will be deposited in the Boating and Waterways
Fund (Fund 608-52-545-000-0000-000-472-612990).

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Each year, approximately ten (10) vessels get abandoned by their owners at the
Berkeley Marina because they lack funds to repair the vessels or they lack funds to pay
for their dockage fees. Due to the age and neglect of the vessels, they have no value,
are not sea-worthy, and are likely to sink. These vessels occupy slips in the Berkeley
Marina that could otherwise be used to generate dockage revenue for the City, and
these vessels are a visual blight on our Marina and harm our reputation. This new
round of funding will assist us as we work to keep our docks clear of derelict vessels in
the coming year, and build upon the progress we make in removing derelict vessels via
previous SAVE Grants.

Effective January 1, 2026, local agencies are required to satisfy noticing requirements
for certain contracts for services that meet the criteria outlined in Government Code



                2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                        E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/
                                                                                                     Page 101
                                           Page 2 of 4

Grant Application: SAVE grant for abandoned vessels                     CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                            October 27, 2026


Section 3504.1 as amended by AB 339. This project does not meet the criteria in
Government Code Section 3504.1 and is exempt from the noticing requirement.

BACKGROUND
Responsibility for derelict and abandoned vessels, unfortunately, often falls on public
agencies. Over time, the City has been awarded the following SAVE grants to remove
derelict vessels:

      In 2020, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $130,000 and
       removed 25 derelict vessels.
      In late 2020, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $42,000 and
       removed eight derelict vessels.
      In late 2021, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $42,000 and
       removed seven vessels.
      In late 2022, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $60,000 and
       removed 16 vessels.
      In late 2023, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $60,000 and
       removed 16 vessels.
      In late 2024, the Berkeley Marina was awarded a SAVE grant for $50,000 and
       removed nine vessels.
      In late 2025, the Berkeley Marina was awarded another grant for $10,000 and
       removed one vessel.

For the past 20 years, the Division of Boating and Waterways has provided grant
funding assistance to public agencies throughout California, including the City of
Berkeley, to properly remove, store, and dispose of abandoned, wrecked, or dismantled
vessels or any other partially submerged objects that pose a substantial hazard to
navigation, from navigable waterways or adjacent public property, or private property
with the landowner’s consent.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
Derelict, abandoned, and sunken vessels pose a navigational and environmental
hazard to the waters of the Bay (e.g., they can leak oil fuel, oil coolant, paints and
solvents, sanitary waste, etc.) Removal and proper disposal of these vessels
contributes to the improvement to the health of the Bay waters.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The City’s Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Department has the primary responsibility
for removing derelict and abandoned vessels from local waters. SAVE grants allow the
City to substantially leverage our existing funding to safely remove potential
environmental and navigational hazards from our waters. The swift removal of derelict
vessels from our Marina via SAVE Funds prevents the accumulation of such vessels on
our docks improves the attractiveness of the Berkeley Marina to existing and
prospective slip holders. This project advances the Strategic Plan goal to provide state-
of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Securing OTS grant funding is a Strategic Plan Priority Project that advances the City’s
goal of fostering a resilient, safe, connected, and prepared community.

The Traffic Bureau within the Berkeley Police Department is currently staffed by two
motor officers, one traffic data analyst, one Sergeant, and one Lieutenant. Motor officers

BACKGROUND
Office of Traffic Safety (OTS) rankings place the City of Berkeley number one for seven
of the last eight years in pedestrian and bicycle related injury collisions when compared
to sixty-two other cities with similar populations. Each year, hundreds of people are
injured in traffic collisions in Berkeley. The City also consistently ranks high in total fatal
and injury collisions, hit-and-run injury collisions, speed-related collisions, nighttime
collisions, and motorcycle-involved collisions. With assistance from the 2027 Office of
Traffic Safety Grant, the department will continue our efforts to reduce the number of
community members injured in collisions —whether they walk, roll, drive, bike, or ride a
motorcycle in our city.

In 2023, OTS data shows Berkeley ranked:

• 1st out of 62 cities for injury collisions involving pedestrians
• 2nd out of 62 cities for collisions involving bicyclists
• 3rd out of 62 cities for collisions involving pedestrians age 65+
• 8th out of 62 cities for collisions involving motorcyclists

Based on these rankings, Berkeley remains one of the most dangerous cities in
California for pedestrians or bicyclists.

Between 2015 through 2025, The City experienced 34 fatal auto collisions. Of these
fatalities, 20 involved pedestrians, 4 involved bicyclists, and 4 involved drugs or alcohol
as contributing factor.

The OTS Grant directly aligns with the City Council’s Vision Zero Program, which aims
to eliminate severe and fatal traffic injuries. The grant supports two of Vision Zero’s
three core tenets: Public Awareness/Education and Traffic Enforcement. Public
awareness efforts include social media messaging, departmental updates, and direct
engagement with community members in the field and at public meetings. Traffic
enforcement is conducted through data-driven strategies focused on primary collision
factor violations in areas where they are most likely to occur. Together, these efforts
strengthen Berkeley’s commitment to roadway safety and injury prevention.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The City of Berkeley continues to have one of the highest bicycle and pedestrian usage
rates in the Alameda County. As a result, a significant number of bicyclists and
pedestrians regularly share the roadway with motorists. This grant supports the City’s
efforts to promote sustainable transportation choices that reduce greenhouse gas
emissions, while also advancing the goal of reducing traffic-related injuries and fatalities
across all modes of transportation.

                 Program (HSIP) Cycle-13 Grant Application and to execute any resultant

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a resolution authorizing the City Manager to submit an application by November
2, 2026 to the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) for a Local Highway
Safety Improvement Program (HSIP) Cycle-13 grant for safety improvements to thirty
(30) signalized intersections along Shattuck Avenue, University Avenue, Bancroft Way,
and Oxford Street; accept the funds; and execute any resultant agreements and
amendments.

SUMMARY
On November 2, 2026, the City of Berkeley Public Works Transportation Division will
submit a Local Highway Safety Improvement Program (HSIP) Cycle-13 grant
application to the California Department of Transportation: the Berkeley Vision Zero
Signal Safety Improvement Project. This project proposes to make systemic traffic
signal safety improvements at 30 signalized intersections along: Shattuck Avenue
between Rose and Ward streets; University Avenue between Milvia and Bonar streets;
Bancroft Way between Telegraph Avenue and Fulton Street; and, Oxford Street
between Hearst and Center streets.

Proposed improvements include upgrading traffic signal heads and backplates;
installing or upgrading smart detection cameras, accessible pedestrian signals (APS),
traffic signal cabinets, controllers and related signal hardware; optimizing signal timing
and phasing for improved safety and operations; and, implementing protected left-turn
phasing at locations where existing left-turn lanes and intersection conditions support
the improvement. This technology stack of smart cameras, cabinets, controllers and
other hardware will allow electricians to monitor traffic signal operations in real-time,
identify and improve traffic management issues, understand road users’ intersection
movements, and improve signal timing and safety for people on foot, bicycle, in cars
and on public transit.

These improvements, along some of the City's busiest transportation corridors, would
benefit a broad range of Berkeley road users, including pedestrians, bicyclists, transit
riders, motorists, young people, elders, and people with disabilities. The improvements
are intended to reduce the potential for severe crashes, improve pedestrian and
bicyclist visibility and detection, reduce conflicts between turning drivers and other
roadway users, and modernize aging signals, some of which are over 50 years old.

The project would also support the City's Vision Zero goal to eliminate traffic fatalities
and severe injuries by prioritizing safety improvements at locations with documented
collision histories and roadway safety needs. All of the proposed locations are on
Berkeley’s network of Vision Zero high-injury streets -- these are the 15-percent of
Berkeley roads that account for over 80-percent of severe and fatal crashes.

Approximately $370-million in funding is available statewide through Caltrans for HSIP
Cycle-13. Approval of the resolution would authorize and support the City's application
for HSIP Cycle-13 funding for the proposed traffic signal safety improvement project.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
If the Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project is awarded HSIP Cycle-
13 funding, Caltrans would provide up to $6,335,550 in grant funds, which would be
accounted for in the City’s Fund 306-Capital Grants-State. The program requires a 10-
percent local match based on the total project cost, resulting in a required City
contribution of $703,950. Funding for the local match would be available beginning in
Fiscal Year 2028/2029 from Measure FF (Fund 166).

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project addresses safety needs at
30 signalized intersections along Shattuck Avenue, University Avenue, Bancroft Way,
and Oxford Street. These corridors are major multimodal routes serving pedestrians,
bicyclists, transit riders, and motorists. They are all designated through Berkeley’s
Vision Zero Action Plan as high-injury streets – priority focus areas for safety
investments.

Existing conditions vary by location and include aging or outdated signal equipment,
limited detection capabilities, signal visibility concerns, turning conflicts, and
opportunities to improve signal timing and phasing. Collision history at the project
intersections further demonstrates the need for targeted safety improvements.

Without additional investment, many of these safety and operational deficiencies would
need to be addressed incrementally or not at all using limited local funding. HSIP Cycle-
13 provides an opportunity to implement coordinated improvements across multiple
high-priority corridors and accelerate upgrades intended to reduce fatal and severe-
injury collisions.

BACKGROUND
The Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project is a systemic traffic signal
safety project focused on 30 signalized intersections along Shattuck Avenue, University
Avenue, Bancroft Way, and Oxford Street. Together, the project locations encompass
approximately 4.9-miles of roadway along corridors identified by the City as part of its
network of high-injury streets. The project will address recurring intersection crash
patterns through targeted improvements to existing traffic signal infrastructure and
operations.

The City’s HSIP Cycle-13 grant application safety analysis uses collision data from the
Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System (SWITRS) and UC Berkeley SafeTREC
Transportation Injury Mapping System (TIMS) in combination with estimated crash
reduction benefits for various treatments in order to calculate the application’s “Benefit-
Cost Ratio”. This ratio is the primary criterion for project funding decisions.

For the five-year period from January 1, 2021 through January 1, 2026, the 30 project
intersections experienced 432 reported crashes, including 1 fatal crash, 41 severe-injury
crashes, 296 other visible-injury crashes, and 94 complaint-of-pain crashes. This
represents 42 fatal or severe-injury crashes at the proposed project locations during the
analysis period.

Based on this collision history, staff analysis, and the crash reduction benefits assigned
by the HSIP program to various treatments, the project proposes three primary
countermeasures: signal hardware, signal timing, and protected left-turn phasing (i.e.,
dedicated left-turn arrows). These improvements would be applied at locations
supported by collision patterns, roadway conditions, existing signal configurations, and
engineering analysis rather than applying the same treatment uniformly at every
intersection.

Proposed improvements include replacement or installation of signal heads and
backplates with retroreflective borders, pedestrian countdown indications, accessible
pedestrian signal equipment, smart detection cameras, traffic signal cabinets and
controllers, and other related signal hardware. The project would also optimize signal
timing and phasing and install protected left-turn phasing and associated equipment at
locations where existing left-turn lanes and intersection conditions allow. The HSIP cost
estimate currently identifies protected left-turn improvements at 16 intersections, signal
hardware improvements at 28 intersections, and signal timing improvements at all 30
project intersections.

The proposed improvements are intended to reduce the frequency and severity of
intersection crashes, improve signal visibility and detection, reduce conflicts associated
with turning movements, and modernize existing traffic signal infrastructure. By pursuing
these improvements through a coordinated, systemic project, the City can address
common safety needs across several priority corridors.

The project is also consistent with the City’s 2020 Vision Zero Action Plan and 2020
Pedestrian Plan, which establish City priorities for reducing fatal and severe-injury
collisions and improving pedestrian safety and accessibility throughout Berkeley. The
proposed HSIP improvements advance goals in these adopted plans by directing
investment toward high-injury corridors and implementing proven signal-related safety
countermeasures. The project further supports the City’s broader Vision Zero and Safe
System approach by using collision data and engineering analysis to prioritize
improvements that reduce the likelihood and severity of crashes.

This Local Highway Safety Improvement Program (HSIP) Cycle-13 Grant Application to
fund the Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project advances the
Strategic Plan goal to provide state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities,
and facilities.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project supports the City’s
environmental sustainability and climate goals by improving the safety and operation of
major multimodal transportation corridors. The Berkeley Climate Action Plan establishes
a citywide goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 80-percent below 2000 levels by
2050 and identifies public transit, walking, bicycling, and other sustainable mobility
options as important components of achieving the City’s climate objectives.

Improving the safety and reliability of the City’s multimodal transportation network
supports continued use of walking, bicycling, and public transit as alternatives to single-
occupancy vehicle travel. Modernized signal controllers, detection systems, and
optimized signal timing can also improve traffic operations by reducing unnecessary
delays and vehicle idling. This is consistent with the City’s Climate Action Plan, Vision
Zero Action Plan, Pedestrian Plan, and Bicycle Plan. The City’s current adopted
transportation plans identify improving safety and expanding sustainable transportation
choices as complementary objectives.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Adoption of the Resolution would allow the City to pursue up to $6,335,550 in HSIP
Cycle-13 funding for the Berkeley Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project. The
grant would leverage Measure FF funding for the required local match and allow the
City to accelerate safety improvements that would otherwise need to compete for limited
local transportation funding.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
Staff considered a range of potential transportation safety projects and eligible
countermeasures for submission under HSIP Cycle-13 before selecting the Berkeley
Vision Zero Signal Safety Improvement Project. The proposed project was selected
because it provides a competitive Benefit-Cost Ratio that maximizes the chance for
funding, while addressing safety on multiple high-priority corridors.

Staff considered implementing these improvements using local funding sources.
However, relying solely on local funds would require the improvements to be phased

implementation of priority traffic signal upgrades.

Council could choose not to adopt the Resolution, in which case the City would forego
the opportunity to compete for HSIP Cycle-13 funding for this project.

Subject:         Authorize the City Manager to Negotiate and Execute a Project Specific
                 Maintenance Agreement between the California Department of
                 Transportation and City of Berkeley for the San Pablo Avenue Safety
                 Enhancements Project

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to negotiate and execute a Project
Specific Maintenance Agreement (PSMA) and any extensions and amendments with
the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) for maintenance of City
improvements installed in the state highway during Alameda County Transportation
Commission’s (ACTC) San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project.

SUMMARY
The Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC) is making road safety and
mobility improvements on San Pablo Avenue between Heinz Avenue and the Berkeley-
Albany border. ACTC’s project is based on approved City plans and extensive
community outreach. ACTC is making these improvements at no cost to the City. As a
condition of this investment, the City is required commit to maintain these
improvements, even though San Pablo Avenue is a state route under the jurisdiction of
Caltrans.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The PSMA commits the City to maintain the identified improvements installed along
San Pablo Avenue (State Route 123) under ACTC’s San Pablo Avenue Safety
Enhancements Project. There would be no reimbursement from Caltrans for the City’s
efforts on maintaining the items identified in the PSMA such as Rectangular Rapid
Flashing Beacons (RRFBs), Pedestrian Hybrid Beacons (PHBs), pedestrian scale
lighting, green bike lane striping, bus shelters, benches, trash cans, and bike racks.

The design and construction of the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project
is fully funded by ACTC. The City’s contribution is the commitment to pay for the long-
term maintenance of certain improvements installed by the project, through the
proposed PSMA. The City funds Public Works maintenance activities from Measure
BB, Fund 134, and Vehicle Registration Fee (VRF) direct local distribution funds, Fund
