CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
This Project Specific Maintenance Agreement between the California Department of
Transportation and City of Berkeley for the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements
Project advances the Strategic Plan goal to provide state-of-the-art, well-maintained
infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.

On November 14, 2023, City Council approved Resolution No. 71,097-N.S. authorizing
the City Manager to direct staff to partner with ACTC on the final design and
implementation of the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project. The project will
improve transit operations along San Pablo Avenue and safety for bicycle and
pedestrian crossings of San Pablo Avenue in Berkeley and Albany.

The project includes bus bulbs and pads, relocating bus stops, Americans with
Disabilities Act-compliant curb ramp and signal upgrades, high-visibility cross walk
markings, pedestrian lighting upgrades, new pedestrian hybrid beacons (PHBs), and
new rectangular rapid flashing beacons (RRFBs). This segment of the project is on San
Pablo Avenue from Heinz Avenue to the Berkeley-Albany border. City streets that
connect to San Pablo Avenue will also experience construction-related improvements
as part of corner curb ramps and drainage upgrades.

Between 2022 and 2026, staff from Public Works Transportation, Engineering, ADA,
Operations and Maintenance, and Zero Waste along with technical advisory
committee (TAC) members from the Fire Department, Police Department, and PRW
Urban Forestry reviewed design and engineering packages. In May 2026 the City’s
TAC completed review of the final design plans, enabling Caltrans to proceed with
advertising the project for construction.

ACTC is expected to start construction on the project in spring 2027 and take up to
two years to finish.

BACKGROUND
ACTC initiated engagement with the City and Caltrans to improve safety, transit
performance, and adding Complete Streets design elements to the San Pablo corridor
following adoption of the Countywide Transportation plan in 2020. San Pablo Avenue
is on the countywide High Injury Network and identified in the City’s 2020 Vision Zero
Action Plan as a high injury street. San Pablo Avenue in Berkeley is in an Equity
Priority Community (EPC) and a Priority Development Area (PDA) planned for growth
and increased density. All of these factors were considered when Council approved
Resolution No 71,097-N.S. on November 14, 2023 authorizing the City Manager to
partner with ACTC on the final design and implementation of the San Pablo Avenue
Safety Enhancements Project.

The project underwent five rounds of review with City staff at various stages of design,
and City Council approved the conceptual design for the project in November 2023.
Numerous city departments and divisions within Public Works participated in the
review process to ensure that the project fully supports City plans, policies and
requirements. The final review was completed in May 2026.

Maintenance, as defined by Caltrans, is the preservation and keeping of right-of-way,
and each type of roadway structure safety convenience or device, planting,
illumination equipment, and other facility, in the safe and usable condition to which it
has been improved or constructed, but does not include reconstruction or other major
improvement.

The City and Caltrans have negotiated the terms of the PSMA, but legal review to
finalize the agreement remains and is not expected to materially change the terms of
the agreement attached to this staff report.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Ongoing maintenance of the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project will help
more people move through Berkeley by foot, bicycle, scooter, transit and other low- and
no-carbon modes of transportation. Building and maintaining this project supports the
City’s adopted Climate Action Plan, which aims to make transit, walking, cycling, and
other sustainable mobility modes the primary means of transportation for Berkeley
residents and visitors by 2050. This project also supports other City adopted plans,
including but not limited to the ADA Transition Plan, Age-Friendly Berkeley Action Plan,
Bicycle Plan, Electric Mobility Roadmap, Pedestrian Plan and Vision Zero Action Plan.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
ACTC must obtain an encroachment permit from Caltrans in order to perform
construction work in the State’s right of way for the San Pablo Avenue Safety
Enhancements Project, and Caltrans requires that a PSMA be executed prior to issuing
the encroachment permit.

Therefore, in order to proceed with construction, Council needs to authorize the City
Manager to finalize negotiations and execute the PSMA with Caltrans to maintain the
project improvements installed in the state highway.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
Council could not to authorize execution of a PSMA and ACTC would need to cancel
implementation of San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project. Public Works staff
have reviewed and limited the City’s commitments in the PSMA to only non-standard
features to support safe walking, biking, and transit use along the corridor.

                            RESOLUTION NO. ##,###-N.S.

  AUTHORIZE THE CITY MANAGER TO NEGOTIATE AND EXECUTE A PROJECT
     SPECIFIC MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CALIFORNIA
  DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION AND CITY OF BERKELEY FOR THE SAN
           PABLO AVENUE SAFETY ENHANCEMENTS PROJECT


WHEREAS, the Alameda County Transportation Commission’s (ACTC) funding and
construction of the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements Project will improve
safety and accessibility for people walking, biking and taking transit along the busy
San Pablo Avenue corridor between Heinz Avenue and the jurisdictional boundary of
Berkeley and Albany; and

WHEREAS, this project includes improvements within the State of California right of
way on Highway 123 (San Pablo Avenue); and

WHEREAS, the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) requires ACTC to
apply for an encroachment permit prior to performing any work within the State right of
way; and

WHEREAS, Caltrans requires the execution of a Project Specific Maintenance
Agreement (PSMA) for maintenance of local improvements within State highways
such as rectangular rapid flashing beacons, pedestrian hybrid beacons, green
bikeway pavement markings, pedestrian scale lighting, benches, trash receptacles,
bus shelters, and bike racks as a precondition to issuing an encroachment permit; and

WHEREAS, the City receives Measure BB and Alameda County Vehicle Registration
Fee (VRF) funds to support paying for maintenance of local transportation
improvements; and

WHEREAS, City staff and Caltrans have negotiated the terms of a PSMA and the final
legal reviews are not anticipated to materially change the nature of the negotiated
agreement.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Council of the City of Berkeley
authorizes the City Manager to finalize negotiations and execute a Project Specific
Maintenance Agreement (PSMA) and any extensions and amendments with the
California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) for maintenance of specific
identified improvements constructed during the San Pablo Avenue Safety Enhancements
Project. A record signature copy of the PSMA will be on file in the Office of the City
Clerk.

Office of the City Manager
                                                                           CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jamie Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:         Contract No. 32300096 Amendment: SCS Engineers for Landfill Post-Closure
                 Maintenance and Monitoring Services

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute an amendment to Contract
No. 32300096 with SCS Engineers for maintenance, monitoring, and compliance services
related to the closed landfill, increasing the contract amount by $1,600,000 for a total not
to exceed amount of $5,678,022.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Funding for this amendment in the amount of $1,600,000 is available in FY 2027 in the
Zero Waste Fund (601).

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The City relies on the resources and expertise of qualified consultants to maintain the
landfill gas collection and flare system at the closed landfill located at the park at the
Berkeley Waterfront, and to monitor surface and subsurface conditions at the closed
landfill in compliance with regulatory agencies.

The current contract with SCS Engineers ("SCS") for landfill post-closure maintenance,
monitoring, and compliance services was authorized by Council on September 20, 2022
by Resolution No. 70,532-N.S. The contract was originally executed for a term of
January 1, 2023 to June 30, 2026. Amendments to the current contract were authorized
by Council on May 14, 2024 by Resolution No. 71,330-N.S and on July 29, 2025 by
Resolution No. 71,917-N.S. increasing the contract amount to an amount not to exceed
$4,078,022. The amended contract amount provides for routine maintenance and
Abatement Order compliance services through October 2026.

The amendments were triggered by a series of Notices of Violations (“NOVs”) issued by
the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) Board to the City, preparations
for a variance request to BAAQMD for these violations, and a subsequent hearing with
the BAAQMD Hearing Board. Following the hearing, the BAAQMD denied the City’s
variance request and issued an Abatement Order (Order). The order mandated

Contract No. 32300096 Amendment:                                       CONSENT CALENDAR
SCS Engineers for Landfill Post-Closure                                    October 27, 2026
Maintenance and Monitoring Services




compliance actions and conditions beyond routine monitoring and maintenance activities
that City staff can accomplish.

Additional contract authority is required to extend routine maintenance and monitoring
services and additional year of Abatement Order related compliance monitoring through
the extended contract deadline of June 30, 2027, perform one-time permitting and
construction tasks identified during previous Abatement Order required investigatory
work, and to perform tasks required to fulfill the City's Work Plan to address elevated
leachate levels, which was approved in January 2026.

Along with Abatement Order work, routine maintenance and monitoring activities continue
to be required for the closed landfill to complete routine compliance tasks and regulatory
submittals.

These actions and improvements are estimated to require $1,600,000 in additional
funding through the end of Fiscal Year 27.

The services provided by the SCS contract support the Strategic Plan goal of providing
state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.

BACKGROUND
The park at the Berkeley Waterfront is located at the Berkeley Marina on the site of the
former ninety-acre Berkeley Landfill. The park has been open to the public for recreational
use since 1991. BAAQMD issued the City of Berkeley an operations permit for a Landfill
Post Closure Monitoring and Maintenance Program to monitor and maintain the landfill
gas collection system, groundwater wells, leachate wells, and other surface and
subsurface conditions in accordance with Air District, CalRecycle and State Regional
Water Quality Control Board regulations. Landfill post-closure compliance services will be
required for a forty to fifty-year period before the site can be deemed permanently closed.

Beginning on November 22, 2021, BAAQMD issued a series of NOVs related to non-
compliant operation of the landfill gas collection system. On February 6, 2024, BAAQMD
voted to issue an Abatement Order which requires the City to take a series of compliance
actions to bring the closed landfill to full compliance. Actions include locating missing gas
collection wells, testing, repairs of the gas collection system; and the development and
implementation of a process to identify any gas seeping offsite.

In addition to the Abatement Order, the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality
Control Board (RWQCB) issued various requirements for the City for radiological testing
at the closed landfill and reports summarizing the testing results and a requirement to
address elevated leachate levels in the subsurface gas collection system. The
radiological testing requirements are based on a January 18, 2024 letter from the
RWQCB indicated that industrial waste materials from the Stauffer Chemical Company
(later known as Zeneca) Richmond Plant may have been disposed at the former landfill
between 1960 and 1971. The requirement to address elevated leachate levels is a result

Contract No. 32300096 Amendment:                                      CONSENT CALENDAR
SCS Engineers for Landfill Post-Closure                                   October 27, 2026
Maintenance and Monitoring Services




of an October 3, 2024, letter from RWQCB indicating that leachate must be collected and
removed from the gas wells to allow proper function of the gas collection and flare system.


This contract is exempt from AB 339, which requires noticing of contract work to local
public employee unions. Section 3504.1 of the California Government code explicitly
states in Section 1(d) (1), that AB 339 does not apply to the contracting of services
related to, “…the planning, design, administration, oversight, review, or delivery of
public works, …or other infrastructure projects subject to adopted uniform codes or
standards.”

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Hiring SCS to continue providing landfill post-closure engineering services will help
ensure that greenhouse gases that are emanating from the closed landfill are captured
and incinerated before entering the atmosphere.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The services requested are required to comply with the landfill post-closure operations
permit and the Abatement Order. Continuing with the same contractor ensures ongoing
compliance measures are uninterrupted and consistent. SCS has familiarity with the site
conditions and operations and has long served as the primary contractor for the City’s
closed landfill. Their historic familiarity with both the site and the requirements of the
Abatement Order means that amending their current contract will allow for uninterrupted
work towards completion of all regulatory compliance tasks at the closed landfill. The City
lacks the in-house expertise or resources needed to fulfill these obligations.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
No alternative action was considered since compliance with federal, state, and regional
regulatory requirements is mandatory.

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute a contract amendment with
POSM Software LLC for Pipeline Observation System Management software
maintenance and technical support, extend the contract through October 31, 2028,
increase the contract amount by $40,000 for a total not to exceed $88,650, and waiving
competitive solicitation requirements on a sole-source basis.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Funding is available in the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 adopted budget in Fund 611 and Fund
616. Funding for the portion of the contract occurring in FY 2028 and FY 2029 is subject
to Council’s approval of the proposed citywide budgets.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Software maintenance, updates, and technical support are necessary to ensure the
reliable operation of the City’s Pipeline Observation System Management (POSM)
software. The software supports the City’s two IBAK closed-circuit television (CCTV)
camera vans and manages wastewater pipeline inspection data collected by the
equipment.
Contract No. 32300167 expires on October 31, 2026. The existing contract has a not-to-
exceed amount of $48,650, which was below the $50,000 threshold requiring City
Council approval. The proposed amendment would extend the contract through October
31, 2028 and increase the contract amount by $40,000, for a total not-to-exceed amount
of $88,650.
The proposed amendment will increase the contract amount above $50,000 and
therefore requires City Council approval. Staff recommends waiving competitive
solicitation requirements on a sole-source basis because POSM Software LLC
exclusively provides the proprietary maintenance and technical support required for the
City’s existing system. Extending the contract for two years will prevent disruptions to
wastewater inspection operations while Public Works completed implementation of its

allow Information Technology staff sufficient time to evaluate an appropriate cloud-

POSM Software LLC for Pipeline Observation System Management software
maintenance and technical support supports the City’s Strategic Plan goal of providing
state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.
Effective January 1, 2026, local agencies are required to satisfy noticing
requirements for certain contracts for services that meet the criteria outlined in
Government Code Section 3504.1 as amended by AB 339. This project does not
meet the criteria in Government Code Section 3504.1 and is exempt from the
noticing requirement.

BACKGROUND
The City entered into Contract No. 32300167 with POSM Software LLC for software
installation, configuration, training, maintenance, and technical support. The agreement
was executed on May 18, 2023, for a term beginning November 1, 2022, and expiring
October 31, 2025. The City subsequently extended the contract through October 31,
2026.
The current contract has a current not-to-exceed amount of $48,650. The proposed two-
year amendment would increase the total contract amount to $88,650, requiring City
Council approval. The City did not conduct a new competitive solicitation or use a
cooperative purchasing agreement because POSM Software LLC develops and
supports the proprietary software currently used by the City. Staff therefore
recommends that Council waive competitive solicitation requirements on a sole-source
basis.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Continued POSM software maintenance and technical support will enable the City to
manage video footage and inspection data collected by its camera vans. This
information helps the City identify sewer pipeline problems, prioritize maintenance and
repairs, prevent potential failures, and use public resources efficiently.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Approval of the two-year amendment will maintain uninterrupted software maintenance,
updates, and technical support for the City’s wastewater pipeline inspection operations
while Public Works completes implementation of its new telematics system and
Information Technology evaluates an appropriate cloud-based pipeline-inspection
solution. POSM Software LLC is the sole source for vendor-level support of its
proprietary software; therefore, continuing the existing contract is the most practical way
to maintain system functionality during this transition.

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jordan Klein, Director, Planning and Development
              Jamie Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:         Ordinance Vacating and Authorizing Transfer of Property Adjacent to the
                 North Berkeley BART TOD Site

RECOMMENDATION
  1. Adopt first reading of an Ordinance (a) declaring four small pieces of land
     described in Exhibit A and shown in Exhibit B, adjacent to the North Berkeley
     BART Transit Oriented Development (TOD), to be exempt surplus land; (b)
     summarily vacating two of the areas that are presently public right of way; and (c)
     approving the transfer of all four areas to the San Francisco Bay Area Rapid
     Transit District (BART);

      2. Upon conclusion of the second reading of the Ordinance, authorize the City
         Manager to execute quitclaim deeds conveying the four areas described in
         Exhibit A and shown in Exhibit B.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Fees associated with processing the proposed street vacations and property transfers
offset the City’s costs related to processing and implementing the recommended action.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The application submitted by the North Berkeley Housing Partners for the North
Berkeley BART Transit-Oriented Development project (the Project) pursuant to AB 2011
(Government Code Section 65912) at 1750 Sacramento (PLN2024-0010) was approved
on December 11, 2024. Approval of this project included approval of Tentative Tract
Map #8713 for the subdivision of 7.88 acres into 12 parcels for residential, open space,
public access, and BART facilities. In addition, Tentative Tract Map #8713 included four
small areas, totaling approximately 1,279 square feet, along Sacramento, Delaware,
and Acton streets adjacent to the North Berkeley BART property to be transferred from
the City to BART. Four areas are proposed for transfer from the City to BART. Two of
these four areas, totaling approximately 165 square feet, are proposed for street
vacation (“Street Vacation Areas”), and the remaining two areas, totaling approximately
1,114 square feet, are not presently in the right-of-way and are proposed for property




    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/
                                                                                                     Page 153
                                                Page 2 of 20

Ordinance Vacating and Authorizing Transfer of Property              CONSENT CALENDAR
Adjacent to the North Berkeley BART TOD Site                             October 27, 2026




transfer (“Transfer Areas”), as shown in the attached legal descriptions and plats
(Exhibit A).

BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Division 9, Part 3, Chapter 4 of the Streets and Highways Code of the State
of California, a local agency may summarily vacate excess right-of-way of a street or
highway when the excess is not required for street or highway purposes and does not
contain in-place public utility facilities that are in use and would be affected by the
vacation. The Streets and Highways Code allows the local agency to summarily vacate
the right-of-way by the adoption of a resolution of vacation.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The impacts of development consistent with the City Code, such as the Project, were
considered in the Ashby and North Berkeley BART Stations Transit-Oriented
Development (TOD) Zoning Project Environmental Impact Report (SCH #:
2020110320), which was certified by the City Council on June 2, 2022 (Zoning EIR).
The vacation and conveyances recommended here are not substantial changes to the
Project; moreover, there has been no substantial change to the circumstances of the
Project nor has new information of substantial importance become available since the
certification of the Zoning EIR. No further environmental review is required pursuant to
CEQA Guidelines section 15162.

As for the vacations and transfers, it can be seen with certainty that there is no
possibility that transferring ownership of a very small area of paved land may have a
significant effect on the environment. Therefore, the vacation and conveyance are not
subject to CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines section 15061.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The vacation and transfer areas are necessary to reconcile existing property and right-
of-way boundaries with the approved Tentative Tract Map (TTM) #8713. Approval will
allow BART, the City, and the developer to prepare a report for Council consideration to
approve a Final Map and associated land dedications. These actions will allow EBALDC
to proceed with recording the Final Map and implementation of the approved project.
The public benefits from the Project, including the construction of affordable housing
and other community benefits proposed for the site, are equal to or greater than the de
minimis value of the lands to be conveyed.

The Planning and Development Department has reviewed the proposed street vacation
and transfers for consistency with the approved TTM Map #8713. The purpose of the
transfers and vacations shown in TTM #8713 and set forth in this item for final approval
is to fulfill the North Berkeley Objective Design Standards (ODS), which require
widening of sidewalks around the site. The additional width for the widened sidewalks in
the ODS results in a shifting of the back of the sidewalk into the site (BART parcels) and
not into the right-of-way. The transfers and vacations move the boundary to the new



                                                    Page 2
                                                                                Page 154
                                                Page 3 of 20

Ordinance Vacating and Authorizing Transfer of Property                            CONSENT CALENDAR
Adjacent to the North Berkeley BART TOD Site                                           October 27, 2026




back of the sidewalk so that each stretch of sidewalk sits in a single ownership. Without
the proposed transfers and vacations shown in TTM #8713, the resulting sidewalk
would be split between City and BART ownership along much of the perimeter. In
addition, the City and BART Joint Vision & Priorities1 sets a goal of narrowing the
perimeter streets and returning them to their original geometry for safety. Consistent
with the JVP, the project straightens Delaware and Acton streets, eliminates the turn
pocket on Acton Street and slightly narrows Delaware Street.

The lands are subject to the Surplus Land Act, California Government Code §§ 54220
et seq. Prior to conveying them out of City ownership, the City must either declare them
to be “exempt surplus land” or undertake procedures to offer them for development as
affordable housing or open space. These lands fit the definition of “exempt surplus
lands,” because they are being conveyed to the adjacent landowner, a state agency,
(BART) and/or because they are a “former street, right-of-way, or easement” being
conveyed to an owner of an adjacent property. See Gov. Code sections 54221(f)(1)(D)
and 54221(f)(1)(E). Therefore, the City may convey them to BART without undertaking
the longer Surplus Land Act processes.

The Public Works Department has reviewed the proposed vacation areas pursuant to
the California Streets and Highways Code §§ 8330 to 8336, and determined that the
segments are excess right-of-way of a street and not required for street purposes.
These segments do not contain in-place public utility facilities that are in use and would
be affected by the vacation. The proposed vacations and transfers will not meaningfully
affect traffic circulation or access in the vicinity of the North Berkeley BART station.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The alternative course of action is to deny the proposed vacations and transfers. Denial
would prevent implementation of the property and right-of-way configuration shown on
the approved Tentative Tract Map and would impede recording the Final Map and
advancement of the approved North Berkeley BART TOD project.

Section 1. Findings. The City Council finds as follows:
   a. The North Berkeley BART Transit-Oriented Development project at 1750
      Sacramento Street was approved on December 11, 2024, including Tentative
      Tract Map No. 8713, which identifies the property and right-of-way configuration
      proposed for the site.
   b. The portions of land described in Exhibit A are small areas located adjacent to
      the North Berkeley BART station site and are proposed to be vacated and/or
      transferred in order to implement the parcel configuration shown on Tentative
      Tract Map No. 8713 and thus to facilitate the project.
   c. The portions of the right-of-way described in Exhibit A are excess right-of-way
      not required for street or highway purposes, pursuant to Streets and Highways
      Code section 8334(a);
   d. The portions of the right-of-way described in Exhibit A do not contain in-place
      public utility facilities that are in use and would be affected by the vacation,
      pursuant to Streets and Highways Code section 8334.5;
   e. The public benefits of the project are equal to or greater than the de minimis
      value of the lands to be conveyed;
   f. The City Clerk is hereby authorized and directed to cause a certified copy of this
      ordinance of vacation, attested by him under seal, to be recorded in the Office of
      the Recorder for Alameda County, California;
   g. The portions of land described in Exhibit A are surplus and not necessary for the
      City’s use. The properties described in Exhibit A are being transferred to another
      state agency, the San Francisco Bay Area Rapid Transit District, and/or are a
      “former street, right-of-way, or easement,” conveyed to an owner of an adjacent
      property. The properties described in Exhibit A are not necessary for the City’s
      use in light of the affordable housing development proposed to be built at the
      North Berkeley BART station site and the corresponding changes to the right of
      way associated with that project.

8330 to 8336, the City of Berkeley hereby vacates the portions of public right-of-way
described in Exhibit A and shown in Exhibit B. From and after the date this ordinance is
recorded, the street, highway, or public service easements vacated no longer constitute
street, highway, or public service easements.

Section 3. Declaration of Exempt Surplus Land.

To:               Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:             Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jamie Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:          Purchase Order: Municipal Maintenance Equipment, Inc. for the Purchase
                  and Installation of a CCTV Sewer Inspection System in One City-Owned
                  Electric Van

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt a Resolution authorizing the City Manager to execute a purchase order with
Municipal Maintenance Equipment, Inc. for the purchase and installation of a closed-
circuit television (CCTV) sewer inspection system in one City-owned electric van in an
amount not to exceed $515,636.69.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
The FY 2027 Adopted Public Works Department Equipment Replacement Fund (Fund
671) budget includes funding for this purchase. The requested $515,636.69
authorization includes the vendor's purchase price of $425,179.71, 10% contingency of
$42,517.97 and estimated sales tax of $47,939.01. Any expenditure exceeding the
authorized not to exceed amount is subject to Council approval.

 Cost Component                                                     Amount
 Municipal Maintenance Equipment, Inc. — Sourcewell contract
                                                                          $425,179.71
 price
 10% Contingency                                                             $42,517.97
 Estimated sales tax (10.25%)                                                $47,939.01
 Total not-to-exceed authorization                                        $515,636.69

The sales-tax amount is an estimate calculated at 10.25 percent of the vendor's
purchase price plus a 10% contingency and is subject to confirmation by Public Works
Administrative and Fiscal staff.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The Public Works Department's existing CCTV sewer inspection van is a 2016 model
and has reached the end of its useful life. Replacing it is necessary to maintain the



                                                                               Page 173
                                                Page 2 of 4

Purchase and Installation of a CCTV Sewer Inspection System            CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026




City's ability to inspect sanitary sewer pipelines, document defects, and make informed
maintenance and repair decisions.

The City previously purchased a 2024 electric Ford Transit cargo van to support another
division’s operational needs. After reassessing its fleet needs, the City determined that
the van is better suited for use as a CCTV sewer inspection vehicle.

Installing a RapidView IBAK high-definition CCTV pipeline inspection system in this
City-owned van is the most cost-effective option because it avoids the need to purchase
another vehicle. The installation will create a complete mobile CCTV sewer inspection
unit with the equipment and vehicle modifications needed to inspect and document the
condition of the City’s sanitary sewer pipelines.

Municipal Maintenance Equipment, Inc.’s proposed purchase price is $425,179.71, 10%
contingency of $42,517.97 plus estimated sales tax of $47,939.01, for a total of
$515,636.69. The purchase includes delivery to Berkeley, installation, round-trip
transportation of the City-owned van to RapidView’s installation facility in Rochester,
Indiana, two days of onsite equipment training, and one day of onsite support to transfer
the City’s POSM Software LLC software license (Pipeline Observation System
Management).

The vendor estimates that delivery will occur 120 to 270 days after receiving the City’s
van, depending on equipment availability and installation scheduling. The purchase will
be made through Sourcewell Master Agreement No. 080525-RVL and will not exceed
the amount authorized by the City Council. This purchase supports the City’s Strategic
Plan goal of providing state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and
facilities.

Effective January 1, 2026, local agencies are required to satisfy noticing requirements
for certain service contracts that meet the criteria established by Government Code
Section 3504.1, as amended by Assembly Bill 339. This purchase does not meet those
criteria and is therefore exempt from the noticing requirement.

BACKGROUND
The City may use pricing obtained through a competitively solicited cooperative
purchasing agreement when procuring goods and services. Sourcewell is a government
cooperative purchasing organization that competitively solicits and awards contracts for
use by participating public agencies.

On June 17, 2025, Sourcewell issued Request for Proposal No. 080525 for
Underground Infrastructure Inspection and Rehabilitation Equipment with Related
Services. The solicitation was nationally advertised for 49 days, and 17 proposals were
submitted. Sourcewell selected RapidView LLC as the highest-ranked responsive and
responsible proposer and awarded Master Agreement No. 080525-RVL effective March
5, 2026. The four-year agreement expires March 4, 2030.



                                                   Page 2
                                                                                Page 174
                                                Page 3 of 4

Purchase and Installation of a CCTV Sewer Inspection System               CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                              October 27, 2026




Municipal Maintenance Equipment, Inc. is RapidView’s authorized local dealer for the
City’s purchase and will provide local warranty and service support for the RapidView
IBAK equipment.

The City will provide its 2024 electric Ford Transit van for the installation, reducing the
total project cost by eliminating the need to purchase another vehicle. The requested
purchase-order authority covers the inspection equipment, specialized vehicle
modifications, transportation, delivery, training, and POSM Software LLC license-
transfer support; it does not include the cost of the van.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The inspection system will be installed in the City’s 2024 electric Ford Transit van,
avoiding tailpipe emissions during vehicle operation. Lithium iron phosphate batteries
and solar panels will support the system’s onboard electrical needs. Clear video footage
and inspection data will help the City identify problems in sewer pipelines, prioritize
maintenance and repairs, and use public resources efficiently.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Installing the proposed system will create a complete mobile CCTV sewer inspection
unit with the equipment, vehicle modifications, training, and software support needed for
sewer inspections. Using an existing City-owned electric van repurposes an available
City asset, maximizes the City’s prior investment, and reduces the total project cost.
Using the competitively solicited Sourcewell contract provides established pricing and
access to the manufacturer’s authorized local dealer for warranty and service support.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The City could choose not to proceed with the installation, procure a different inspection
system, or purchase another van for this purpose. Staff do not recommend these
alternatives because they would delay placing the 2024 electric Transit into service,
prolong reliance on the 2016 inspection van beyond its useful life, or add unnecessary
vehicle-purchase costs. City staff do not have the specialized capacity to complete the
vehicle modifications and integrate the proprietary inspection system in-house.

Commission on Disability
                                                                           CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026

To:     Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:       Commission on Disability
Submitted by:        Kathi Pugh, Chairperson
Subject: Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG)

RECOMMENDATION
The Berkeley City Council shall refer to the City Attorney the requirement to include, in
all City of Berkeley contracts that impact the public right-of-way, a clause that obligates
City contractors to comply with the Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines
(PROWAG).

POLICY COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION
On September 16, 2026, the Facilities, Infrastructure, Transportation, Environment &
Sustainability Committee adopted the following action: M/S/C (Lunaparra/Humbert)
send the item to Council with a Qualified Positive Recommendation to refer the
development of the PROWAG guidelines to the City Manager with the input of the
Commission on Disability. Vote: All Ayes

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Examples of PROWAG contract clauses are readily available to the Office of the City
Attorney. Adoption of this recommendation should not require significant time or
expense.

The City currently has a staff position assigned to investigate, monitor and enforce
PROWAG. The job description of the City’s ADA Program Coordinator states that
“under general supervision” the position is tasked with “implementation of the City’s
ADA program which includes…receiving and investigating grievance, reviewing projects
plans for accessibility, [and] training city staff.”

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Both the ADA Program Coordinator and 311 receive complaints when disabled
pedestrians and wheelchair users confront hazardous conditions in the public right-of-
way. City staff time, significantly by the ADA Program Coordinator, is already used to, in
many cases, successfully secure compliance with PROWAG. In some cases, City
contractors refuse to comply with accessibility guidelines—because the requirement to
comply is not stipulated in their contract. This is often on large, months-long City
projects that significantly alter and disrupt the public right-of-way.



    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/
                                                                                                     Page 177
                                             Page 2 of 3

Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines          CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                         October 27, 2026




Failure to comply with PROWAG creates serious safety hazards for people with
disabilities. At times, wheelchair users are forced into busy streets when PROWAG is
not followed. In 2024-2025, this occurred repeatedly at projects on Bancroft/Fulton,
University and Shattuck Avenues.

In addition, Audible Information Devices that warn blind and low vision individuals about
blocked and alternate routes are rarely used by City contractors or private construction
companies. When employed, these warning devices are frequently useless. They are,
with regularity, incorrectly placed, not operating and inaudible. The routine failure to
address accessibility for blind and low vision pedestrians creates manifestly unsafe
conditions.

The City of Berkeley Public Works Department must develop proactive and effective
educational, monitoring and enforcement systems to ensure that disruptions in the
public right-of-way, whether performed by the City, its contractors, or during private
construction projects, conform to PROWAG standards. When the City is informed of
potential violations, timely investigation and remediation must bring violations into
PROWAG compliance.

With the passage of Measure FF and the significant street redesign projects that will
result, complying with PROWAG technical standards—in both design and
construction—is imperative. Over many years, significant resources will be devoted to
improving the condition and safety of Berkeley streets and sidewalks. Attention to
PROWAG must be the rule—and included in City contracts. When envisioning
Berkeley’s future, Safe Streets must include the safety of people with disabilities.

BACKGROUND
PROWAG defines aspects of the ADA not specified at the time of the groundbreaking
law’s passage in 1990. The ADA never specifically addressed accessibility in areas
deemed the “public right-of-way.” To support implementation of the ADA, the U.S.
Access Board, a federal agency charged with promoting “equality for people with
disabilities through leadership in accessible design and the development of accessibility
guidelines and standards” created PROWAG. These accessibility guidelines were
developed over the past two decades.

PROWAG was entered into the Federal Register in 2023 and adopted by the U.S.
Department of Transportation in 2024. The City of Berkeley’s 2020 Pedestrian Plan,
Appendix B: Engineering and Design Guidance references PROWAG numerous times.
CalTrans uses its technical standards. It is considered best practice. Yet, it does not
hold the force of federally mandated law. Because of this, the City’s ADA Program
Coordinator has indicated that some City contractors are unwilling to follow PROWAG.
This obstacle to securing the rights and safety of people with disabilities can be
overcome by including a PROWAG clause in City contracts.



                                                                                Page 178
                                             Page 3 of 3

Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines            CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026




PROWAG will define the access standards expected by the City of Berkeley in the
public right-of-way. It will make clear the City’s commitment to accessibility guidelines,
empower the ADA Program Coordinator to enforce those guidelines and give the City
legal recourse should contractors fail to comply with the contract.

Yet a contract clause, without monitoring and enforcement of its obligations, is
meaningless. For implementation, this recommendation requires a Public Works
Department committed to the principles and technical standards outlined in PROWAG.
We expect—and the City should secure—this level of accessibility and safety for the
disability community.

The Commission on Disability took the following action at its April 9, 2025 meeting:

Action: Motion(Fischer/Pugh):To approve the recommendation to City Council regarding
the enforcement of PROWAG, with the ability to make small edits regarding Caltrans
and the City’s use of PROWAG.
Votes: Ayes: Walsh, Fischer, Pugh, Sun, Lewkowicz, Mann, and Holloway;.Nays: None
Abstain: None; Unexcused Absence: None; Leave of Absence: Paz

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
None.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The PROWAG Contract Clause recommendation is a Strategic Plan Priority Project,
advancing the City’s goals in multiple areas:
   ● provide state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities;
   ● create a resilient, safe, connected, and prepared city;
   ● champion and demonstrate social and racial equity.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
No alternative actions have been considered.

CITY MANAGER
The City Manager recommends referring this item to the FITES Committee to better
understand the potential costs and time impacts of undertaking the recommendation to
streetscape projects.

CONTACT PERSON
Thomas Gregory, ADA Program Coordinator, Public Works, 510-981-6418

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jamie Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:         Companion Report: Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way Accessibility
                   Guidelines (PROWAG)

RECOMMENDATION
Receive this report on Public Works’ progress responding to the Commission on
Disability’s PROWAG referral and concur with the FITES Committee’s recommendation
to refer development of PROWAG compliance provisions for work in the public right-of-
way (construction-zone access guidelines and City contract language, with City Attorney
review) to the City Manager, with input from the Commission on Disability (CoD).

POLICY COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION
On September 16, 2026, the Facilities, Infrastructure, Transportation, Environment &
Sustainability Committee adopted the following action: M/S/C (Lunaparra/Humbert)
send the item to Council with a Qualified Positive Recommendation to refer the
development of the PROWAG guidelines to the City Manager with the input of the
Commission on Disability. Vote: All Ayes

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
An assessment of comparable jurisdictions conducted in early 2026 found no other
jurisdiction currently committed to full compliance with PROWAG within construction
zones. This was primarily due to PROWAG not yet being fully adopted by the Federal
government and concerns about the level of effort and costs associated with full
compliance. This makes exact cost estimates challenging. However, adding compliance
with PROWAG as a contractual requirement may result in contractors requiring
additional compensation, additional inspection staff to assure compliance, and some
one-time costs across departments to adjust current practices and educate staff.

Staff time for administering the recommendation has not been calculated within the
following potentially impacted departments: City Attorney, Public Works; Parks
Recreation and Waterfront; Planning and Development; and Health Housing and
Community Services. City staff across multiple departments working in project delivery,
permitting and inspections are not currently trained in PROWAG requirements. Training
expenses have not been determined. Public Works ability to enforce PROWAG
compliance will also be limited by having only one Right-of-Way inspector. Additional



    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/
                                                                                                     Page 181

Companion Report: Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way                     CONSENT CALENDAR
Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG)                                          October 27, 2026




inspectors would increase City’s personnel costs and enable the City to proactively
enforce these regulations. .With only one traffic inspector, the City enforcement will be
complaint driven and subject to staff availability. Public Works will assess inspection
staffing needs as part of implementation through a review of the volume of complaints
and observed compliance issues, including whether any portion of additional staff costs
could be covered through relevant inspection fees and/or fines.

Public Works staff have evaluated the contractual, bidding, and specification language
needed to be modified to require PROWAG compliance. Many documents and
procedures across multiple groups and departments will need to be updated. The City
Attorney’s Office will be consulted on all draft contract provisions.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Public Works staff have met on multiple occasions with Commission on Disability
subcommittee members to gather input around complying with PROWAG in
construction zones. The final design of projects within Berkeley are generally compliant
with PROWAG and have been for several years, which the CoD members affirmed.
This achievement represents process improvements in both the Public Works
Department and Planning and Development Department to ensure that approved plans
for improvements in the public right-of-way prioritize accessibility.

CoD’s concerns are primarily focused on maintaining PROWAG compliant access
adjacent to construction sites in the City. These include a large number of sidewalk
closures for new development projects, as well as improper or inadequate signs and
guidance to provide accessible paths of travel through construction zones. Moreover,
Public Works staff have heard from multiple members of the public, including the
Transportation and Infrastructure Commission, expressing concern with both pedestrian
and bicycle detours through construction zones.

State and federal regulations to which cities must adhere do not require compliance with
PROWAG as it is not currently federal law. To require contractor compliance with
PROWAG in construction zones, staff would have to include requirements into our
contracts, specifications, and bid documents.

BACKGROUND
Following CoD review and action in April 2025, the CoD subcommittee approached the
Public Works Department to address accessibility through and adjacent to all
construction sites throughout the City. Public Works had previously started a process in
2023 or earlier to develop guidelines for accommodating pedestrians, cyclists, and
transit riders at construction sites, but the process never concluded.

In early 2026, the Public Works Department updated the prior draft guidelines based on
best practices and to ensure feasibility, and shared them with the CoD subcommittee
and an ad-hoc subcommittee of the Transportation and Infrastructure Commission
(TIC). Following edits based on stakeholder feedback, Public Works is ready to adopt



                                                                                Page 1822
                                          Page 3 of 6

Companion Report: Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way                    CONSENT CALENDAR
Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG)                                         October 27, 2026




Berkeley’s “Pedestrian, Bicycle, and Bus Facility Accommodation in Construction
Zones” guidelines in November l 2026.

Following adoption, these guidelines would apply immediately to Public Works permits
issued for new development sites, and other permitted construction (e.g.; utility
company actions) within the public ROW. Adopted, rather than draft, guidelines are
necessary to enforce contractor compliance.

In addition, Public Works is proceeding with updating language within City contracts, bid
documents, and pre-construction activities to highlight and require PROWAG
compliance at job sites to ensure compliance for City-led construction projects that do
not require permits. These are primarily construction contracts for capital projects
managed by Public Works and Parks, Recreation and Waterfront. Staff anticipates that
incorporating guidance into contract documents will take approximately 6-8 months.

CoD requested modifications to the City’s 311 system to support reporting of PROWAG
compliance issues and violations at construction sites. The CoD subcommittee provided
specific modifications to support this reporting to 311. Public Works evaluated this
request and supports this change. Public Works staff are working across departments to
determine the feasibility of making the necessary system changes to 311.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Compliance with PROWAG in construction zones assures pedestrian access supporting
walking as a viable mode of transportation for more trips. The Accommodation in
Construction Zones guidelines also require improved protection to maintain cycling
access adjacent to construction zones. Cycling and walking are zero emission travel
modes which support the City’s Climate and sustainability goals.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The City anticipates that PROWAG is going to become federal law and is looking to
take proactive steps to comply. Moreover, ensuring that construction zones prioritize
pedestrian and bicycle safety and accessibility is consistent with numerous City of
Berkeley policies. Given the volume of current and anticipated construction projects in
Berkeley, adopting new guidelines is a high priority for the Public Works Department.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
City Council could give direction to delay implementation of PROWAG guidelines
developed by the Public Works Department until federal adoption of PROWAG.

To:              Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:            Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jaime Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:         Companion Report: Enforcement of Public Right-of-Way Accessibility
                   Guidelines (PROWAG)

RECOMMENDATION
The City Manager recommends that the Public Right-of Way Accessibilities Guidelines
item be referred to the Facilities, Infrastructure, Transportation, Environment and
Sustainability Committee for discussion of potential impacts.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
An assessment of comparable jurisdictions that currently adhere to PROWAG would
need to be conducted to begin to understand the costs for implementation and the
potential long-term impact on contracting and timelines for streetscape infrastructure.

Additionally, staff time for the administration of the recommendation has not yet been
calculated within the following potentially impacted departments: City Attorney, Public
Works; Parks Recreation and Waterfront; Planning and Building; Health Housing and
Community Services; and Finance. City staff across multiple departments acting as
project managers serve as contract monitors and are not currently trained in PROWAG
requirements. Training expenses have not yet been determined.

Time to develop the contractual language needed for implementation would additionally
impact the City Attorney’s Office, which has not been consulted to calculate the exact
staff time required or the potential need for an outside contractor to draft the provisions.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
The City Manager recommends that Council refrain from referring this matter to the City
Attorney's Office at this time. Staff would first need to assess capacity to monitor
contractors' adherence to PROWAG and to determine how to take remedial steps if
contractors fail to comply with PROWAG.

PROWAG is not incorporated in state or federal guidelines to which cities are required
to adhere, and there are no funds tied to citywide implementation. If a contractor was
unwilling or unable to comply with PROWAG, staff do not currently have clear protocols
for when or how to terminate the noncompliant contract. Currently, there are no



    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/

protocols for determining if qualified alternative contactors are readily available to fill any
gaps created by non-PROWAG compliant contractors. Adding compliance with
PROWAG as a contractual duty may result in contractors requiring additional
compensation.

Staff have yet to analyze current budgetary constraints to determine if recommended
implementation costs are feasible.

BACKGROUND
The Commission on Disability took the following action at its April 9, 2025 meeting:

Action: Motion(Fischer/Pugh):To approve the recommendation to City Council regarding
the enforcement of PROWAG, with the ability to make small edits regarding Caltrans
and the City’s use of PROWAG.
Votes: Ayes: Walsh, Fischer, Pugh, Sun, Lewkowicz, Mann, and Holloway; Nays: None
Abstain: None; Unexcused Absence: None; Leave of Absence: Paz

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
All future potential City contractors for projects related to lowering carbon emissions
through upgrading the public right of way to encourage pedestrian and bicyclist use,
would be required by the City to adhere to the PROWAG requirements. While many
already do, including this in the contractual language, rather than in the design phase,
may increase costs.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Better understanding the PROWAG project and cost implications would be prudent
ahead of mandating they be made.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
Staff could begin the process to study the cost of implementation, but the time required
for that study would necessitate an outside contractor to supplement current staffing. A
working group consisting of the aforementioned departments impacted by PROWAG
requirements could be convened to begin to determine feasibility. There are not
currently any funds dedicated in the City Budget for a study by an outside contractor or
an interdepartmental working group.

Adopt a Resolution re-naming the park at the northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront as Si

Renaming the park at the northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront will require
replacement signage with an estimated cost of approximately $16,000, which is not
identified in the PRW FY2027-28 budget.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
In the Council agenda for March 24, 2026, Councilmember Kesarwani and co-sponsors
Taplin, Bartlett, and Blackaby made a referral to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront
Commission as follows: Refer to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission to
officially rename Cesar Chavez Park. This referral to the Parks Commission initiates a
community process which should incorporate feedback from the Commemorative
Committee (which initiated the first renaming process of the park in 1994) as well as
input from other community members and stakeholders. We recommend that Dolores
Huerta be among the options considered for renaming (see Attachment 2).

In the Council agenda for April 14, 2026, Mayor Ishii made a referral to the Parks,
Recreation, and Waterfront Commission as follows: Refer to the City Manager and the
Parks Commission the request to develop and implement a plan and identify budget to
rename City of Berkeley locations, events, and the city holiday currently named for
Cesar Chavez and engage with the Chavez/Huerta Commemoration Period partners
and Latinos Unidos de Berkeley to bring back to City Council recommendations for how
the City of Berkeley, may move forward with a name changes that will continue to honor
the legacy of labor organizing and solidarity for farm workers and recognize farm
workers as the backbone of America (see Attachment 2).

Rename the park at northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront as Si Se Puede Park   CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                                     October 27, 2026


In response to the referrals regarding the renaming of the park at the northern end of
the Berkeley Waterfront, at its regular meetings of May 13, June 10, July 8, and
September 10, 2026, the Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Commission agendized this
item and heard public comment on the renaming of the park at the northern end of the
Berkeley Waterfront. The Commission gave deference to the work and
recommendations of the Commemorative Renaming Committee as had been requested
by the City Council in its referral of the matter to the Commission. Per the Council
Naming Policy procedures, on July 8, 2026, the PRW Commission conducted a public
hearing, and on September 10, 2026, took action to recommend that Council rename
the park at the northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront as Si Se Puede Park as
recommended by the Commemorative Renaming Committee. (M/S/C:
Stewart/Granzella/U); Ayes: Abshez; Granzella; Nash; Philip; Rybczynski; Samelson;
Stewart; Noes: none; Absent: Muszynski; Yeo.

BACKGROUND
The Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Commission agendized this item and heard
public comments at its regular meetings in May, June, July, and September of 2026.
Public comments received by the Commission, including the work of the
Commemorative Renaming Committee suggested several possible names (see
Attachment 2).

CITY MANAGER
The City Manager takes no position on the recommendation contained in this report.
The cost of the replacement signage is $16,000, which is not identified in the PRW
FY2027-28 budget. Once the City has identified funds, the signage can be ordered and
installed in a three month period.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
There are no negative environmental impacts were identified as a result of this
recommendation.

RATIONAL FOR RECOMMENDATION
At its regular meetings of May 13, June 10, July 8, and September 10, 2026, the Parks,
Recreation, and Waterfront Commission agendized this item and heard public comment
on the renaming of the park at the northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront. The PRW
Commission concurs with the work of the Commemorative Renaming Committee to
rename the park at the northern end of the Berkeley Waterfront as Si Se Puede Park.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
None

CONTACT PERSON
Allan Abshez, Chair, Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Commission, 310-922-7573
Roger Miller, Secretary, Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission, 510-981-6704

                                                                        CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                        March 24, 2026

TO:                    Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council

FROM:                  Councilmember Rashi Kesarwani (Author), Councilmembers Terry
                       Taplin, Ben Bartlett and Brent Blackaby (Co-Sponsors)

SUBJECT:               Referral to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission to
                       officially Rename Cesar Chavez Park.

RECOMMENDATION
Refer to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission to officially rename Cesar
Chavez Park. This referral to the Parks Commission initiates a community process
which should incorporate feedback from the Commemorative Committee (which initiated
the first renaming process of the park in 1994) as well as input from other community
members and stakeholders. We recommend that Dolores Huerta be among the options
considered for renaming.

And further, direct the City Manager to remove or cover all signage bearing the name
Cesar Chavez from park property as soon as practicable while leaving intact signage
related to directions and park rules.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
On March 18, 2026, The New York Times published an investigation finding extensive
evidence that United Farm Workers (UFW) co-founder Cesar Chavez, now deceased,
sexually abused young girls and women who worked within The Farmworkers
Movement.1 Two women, now in their sixties, described to the Times how the civil rights
icon and leader abused them for years. The investigation, based on interviews with
more than 60 people–including top aides, relatives, and members of the UFW–found
extensive evidence to support their accusations and those raised by several other
women, including Dolores Huerta, working within The Movement.

That same day, Dolores Huerta issued a statement publicly acknowledging the abuse
she had kept secret for the last six decades in the interest of protecting The
Farmworkers Movement.2 Huerta identified herself as a survivor “of violence, of sexual
abuse, of domineering men who saw me, and other women, as property, or things to
control….” Huerta also commented that she carried this secret for years “because
building the movement and securing farmworker rights was my life’s work…I channeled

1
  New York Times, March 18, 2026: “Cesar Chavez, a Civil Rights Icon, Is Accused of Abusing Girls
for Years” https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/18/us/cesar-chavez-sexual-abuse-allegations-ufw.html
2
  Medium, March 18, 2026: “A Statement from Dolores Huerta”
https://medium.com/@dolores_huerta/march-18-2026-e74c20430555

everything I had into advocating on behalf of millions of farmworkers and others who
were suffering and deserved equal rights.”3

That inner strength and dedication to human rights sustained Dolores Huerta throughout
her entire career. In addition to co-leading the UFW, she worked with the Feminist
Majority Foundation to help Latina women become more active within politics, founded
the Dolores Huerta Foundation4 that advocates for social justice issues and
marginalized communities through grassroots organizing and civic engagement, and
has been active in politics by supporting causes such as immigration reform and
LGBTQ rights.

Born on April 10, 1930 in New Mexico, Dolores Huerta grew up mostly in California,
moving to the state during her early elementary school years after her mother divorced
her father. Throughout her life, she has remained active in California-based human
rights issues, starting with her deep involvement supporting farmworkers throughout the
state, continuing on with the Bakersfield-based Dolores Huerta Foundation, as well as
her campaigning for statewide propositions and supporting local politicians. In addition
to her many awards honoring her human rights work, the California State Senate
awarded Ms. Huerta “Outstanding Labor Leader” in 1984. In 2018, then-Governor Jerry
Brown signed into law Assembly Bill 2644, first introduced by Assemblywoman Eloise
Gomez Reyes, designating April 10th Dolores Huerta Day.5

BACKGROUND
Cesar Chavez Park was officially renamed after the labor leader on July 26, 1994 when
the Berkeley City Council passed resolution No. 57,627 N.S. (attached). Before that it
had been called North Waterfront Park. The name change was in recognition of the
labor leader’s influence on the Berkeley community and the rest of the world, and to
commemorate his life’s work for future generations. When news of the sexual abuse
accusations against him surfaced on March 18th, many residents reached out to City
Council inquiring about changing the name of this park, reflecting community members’
current pain and anger that a leader of such significance would use his status to
dominate, silence, and abuse women who worked beside him.

Since the news broke, cities, school districts, and leaders throughout the state and
country have been grappling with the information and the many public facilities and
events that have honored Cesar Chavez. As a once-revered labor hero, many parks,
pathways, streets, murals, schools, and community buildings bear his name as a way to
honor his work and advocacy on behalf of workers. Currently, many city, school board
and state leaders are considering changing the names of the facilities that honor him, as
Berkeleyside and The San Francisco Chronicle have covered.6 State legislators have

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Like others, community leaders in Berkeley are struggling to integrate the painful news
of the accusations against Cesar Chavez while many are also wanting to elevate and
honor Dolores Huerta who shines as a pillar of strength even more so now that we know
she hid her own pain in an effort to focus on support for laborers. Dolores Huerta has
accomplishments as a labor organizer equal to Cesar Chavez, as well as a significant
background advocating for human rights issues. Considering renaming the park for her
would be a fitting tribute to her life and accomplishments and her survivorship..

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
There is no significant environmental impact of this referral. Renaming the park could be
a way of promoting a sense of healing within the community and thus be a way of
advancing a more positive social environment.

FISCAL IMPACT
This referral has no fiscal impact save staff time for the Parks, Recreation and
Waterfront Commission secretary. It is expected that this commission would also
investigate costs for replacement signage to accommodate the renaming.

                                                                    CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          April 14, 2026
To:        Honorable Members of the City Council

From:      Mayor Adena Ishii (Author), and Council Members Lunaparra, Humbert and
           O’Keefe (Co-Sponsors)

Subject:   Referral to the City Manager and the Parks Commission the request to
           develop and implement a plan and identify budget to rename City of Berkeley
           locations, events, and the city holiday currently named for Cesar Chavez, and
           engage with the Chavez/Huerta Commemoration Period partners and Latinos

           the City of Berkeley may move forward with a name changes that will
           continue to honor the legacy of labor organizing and solidarity for farm

RECOMMENDATION
Refer to the City Manager and the Parks Commission the request to develop and
implement a plan and identify budget to rename City of Berkeley locations, events, and
the city holiday currently named for Cesar Chavez and engage with the Chavez/Huerta
Commemoration Period partners and Latinos Unidos de Berkeley to bring back to City
Council recommendations for how the City of Berkeley, may move forward with a name
changes that will continue to honor the legacy of labor organizing and solidarity for farm
workers and recognize farm workers as the backbone of America.

BACKGROUND
Cesar Chavez, the late United Farm Workers (UFW) co-founder and labor leader has
long been an icon and hero to communities across the country. Berkeley has a long
history of honoring the legacy of Cesar Chavez dating back to 1996 by naming the
City’s waterfront park after him and with an official city holiday that aligns with the State
of California holiday. Over the years, the City has worked collaboratively with the Latinx
community, local educational institutions, and community based organizations to
organize commemorative activities that honor Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and farm
workers.




                                                                                   Page 195
                                           Page
                                            Page10
                                                 2 of 2
                                                      64




The following is an initial list of locations and events:
   ● Cesar Chavez Park (1996)
   ● Cesar Chavez Day -March 30/31 (2000 - aligned with the State Holiday)
   ● Chavez/Huerta Tribute Site and Solar Calendar (2011)
   ● Cesar Chavez-Dolores Huerta Commemorative Period (2021)
   ● Cesar Chavez Park Perimeter Trail Project (2024 -aka Olivia Stegman Trail)

On March 18, 2026, the New York Times published an in-depth investigation
documenting extensive evidence that Mr. Chavez groomed and sexually abused young
girls who worked in the farmworker movement1. In the same story it was revealed that
Mr. Chavez raped UFW co-founder Dolores Huerta. After 60 years of silence, Ms.
Huerta, a renowned labor leader and civil rights activist issued a statement with her
personal story recounting how Chavez had raped her and how she stayed silent
because she “believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I
have spent my entire life fighting for.”2

The members of the Berkeley City Council condemns sexual violence and stands with
the survivors who bravely told their story. In light of the in-depth reporting of credible
accusations against Mr. Chavez the City must work on a path forward to remove Cesar
Chavez’s name from city locations, events, and holidays.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
No Impact

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Staff time to develop a plan and cost allocation to change the name.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
No name change

Honorable Mayor and City Councilmembers (with cc to members of the Parks, Recreation and
Waterfront Commission):

Some thoughts on renaming Cesar Chavez Park, from someone who volunteered extensively for the UFW
in the 1970s and was a full-time volunteer 1975-1976: Like many I was shocked to learn of the sexual
assault allegations against Cesar Chavez as reported recently in the New York Times. I was already
disillusioned about the UFW by 1977. I later submitted a lengthy essay to the Farmworker Movement
Documentation Project, whose archives are stored at UC San Diego. In it I did my best to describe my
experiences both positive and negative of that time as a low-level volunteer for "la causa." But while I'd
seen firsthand that in addition to being a brilliant and charismatic organizer, Cesar was a petty tyrant
whose paranoia was becoming more and more damaging to the farmworker cause by the late 1970s, I
never would have predicted sexual abuse, of which he now stands credibly accused. I guess I still bought
his carefully crafted persona as a servant leader who led a life of almost monklike simplicity.

But here's what I'll say to my well-meaning friends who'd simply like to swap out Cesar Chavez's name
with Dolores Huerta's name on streets, parks, and holidays: While Chavez's flaws now include sexual
transgressions, all of the leadership of the UFW, including Huerta, share responsibility for the
hierarchical UFW culture that prohibited debate, mandated silence, and punished even the mildest
questioning, dissent, or truth- telling (witness the staff purges of the late 1970s well documented in books
as well as articles in the LA Times). I have great admiration for Dolores Huerta and the many good causes
she has supported over the decades. And I understand that as a woman of my mother's generation --
their birthdays are one day apart -- there is deeply ingrained conditioning at play. But withholding the
truth about her experience for decades strikes me as not so far removed from the many ways the UFW
leadership, including Huerta, tried to control what could and could not be said through a code of silence
as well as an undemocratic and authoritarian structure.

It's the farmworkers themselves, along with their supporters across the country, who made the
movement. Could it be time to release the idea that we have honor individual heroes rather than the
movements they represent? Can we at long last learn from the flaws not just of one man but of entire
structures? I continue to bow before the many, many individuals I met while working for the UFW, some
depicted in the drawing below. They will always represent to me the best of humanity, whatever the flaws
of the leadership they followed. Together they won important improvements for farmworkers, but much
more remains to be done. I'm grateful to the State of California legislature and governor for renaming this
year's March 31st holiday Farmworkers Day.

I trust you will allow a full community process to unfold as you consider alternate names for our precious
park by the bay. I hope you will refrain from honoring a specific individual as you rename the park.

Farmworkers -- who harvest the food we all eat -- and the movement they built deserve consideration in
that process.

SIncerely yours,
Nancy Carleton

employer. Their primary value was their pre-injury physical abilities. Once injured, these agricultural workers

Following the April 14, 2026, referral by the Mayor,1 members of the Citywide Commemorative
Committee2 constituted a renaming working group in order to submit a recommendation to the
Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commissíon and City Manager for renaming the waterfront
park. The committee of 21 members was drawn from many constituencies and stakeholders,
including representatives from Latinos Unidos, the Multicultural Institute, Berkeley Unified
School District, the Park Conservancy, the Off-Leash Association, the Tribute Síte, the Ecology
Center, UC Berkeley, the mayors and council aides, and community members (see Appendix).

Each individual and constituency brought a unique perspective on the park's history, current
use, and potential. We conducted a substantial deliberative process that included reviewing
the Mayor's referral, consulting city policy on naming and renaming, and developing criteria to
review proposed names before polling representatives and discussing the poll results.

This committee process adapted the successful model developed and refined during recent
BUSD school renaming efforts to carefully consider each name, including its educational
implications and any caveats. We hope you will find this report illuminating for your discussion
and deliberation, and believe you may find this process helpful for your future naming or
renaming work.

We are pleased to have reached a strong consensus on a recommendation for a new name,
one that we believe will endure and inspire our Berkeley community for generations to come:
¡Sí Se Puede! Park. Please read the attached report for supporting details.
