FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Staff in the Zero Waste Division of the Public Works Department, in conjunction with the
Planning Department will research the fiscal impacts for the implementation of a menu
of potential enforcement options and develop an associated cost model for
each option. Assessment of these Fiscal Impacts will require minimal staff time.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
This C&D enforcement referral is a Zero Waste Strategic Plan Priority Project,
advancing the City’s goal to be a global leader in addressing climate change, advancing
environmental justice, and protecting the environment.

Construction waste diversion is the process of redirecting waste materials generated
from C&D debris away from landfills, toward salvage, recycling, and composting.

Berkeley Green Code diversion requirements were adopted in the Berkeley Municipal
Code as Chapter 19.37 in 2025. Chapter 19.37 requires that 65% of
construction and demolition (C&D) material be diverted from landfill, and 100% of
excavated soil, concrete, and asphalt. Reducing the amount of C&D material that goes
to landfill is essential to reducing associated GHG emissions, decreasing land use
needed for landfills, and reducing environmental degradation.

Because there is no consequential mechanism outlined in
the Berkeley Municipal Code to provide guidance in regard to penalizing non-
compliant contractors, staff have difficulty when it comes to ensuring contractors and
haulers comply with diversion requirements. To understand diversion levels in Berkeley,
staff rely on self-
reporting from contractors on Green Halo, a C&D debris diversion tracking platform.
Common issues surrounding compliance include:

   1. Improper source separation to the extent that it impedes meeting C&D debris
      diversion requirements.

   2. Uploading fraudulent weight tickets to the Green Halo platform.

   3. Uploading weight tickets in an untimely manner.

   4. Repeated non-compliance beyond three violations.




                                                                              Page 315
                                         Page 4 of 7

Enforceable Mechanism for Berkeley Green Code Compliance             CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




As a result, 17% of projects in 2025 failed to meet Berkeley Green Code (BMC
19.37) requirements. Figure 1 displays the
rates by project type for all registered projects in the database since 2012. Construction
projects tend to divert the least amount of debris, while stand-alone demolition projects
tend to divert the most.

Proper sorting and bagging ensure that C&D debris remains uncontaminated. Source
separation is particularly important for materials like cement and asphalt so that these
waste streams can achieve their required 100% diversion requirement. Many
contractors transport C&D debris, mixed with residential waste, in black plastic bags–
 leading to recyclable debris being coded as landfill, leading to projects failing to
achieve the 65% C&D diversion requirement. Miscoded tickets also prevent staff from
verifying data, leading to unreliable documentation surrounding C&D
debris diversion and potential missed opportunities to increase diversion.




                                                                                Page 316
                                         Page 5 of 7

Enforceable Mechanism for Berkeley Green Code Compliance             CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




The biggest area where diversion could improve is by penalizing repeat offenders.
Over 40 contractors, who have repeatedly been out of compliance annually for over a
decade, have been identified by staff. Contractors often attempt to reuse or tamper
with weight tickets, causing staff to spend extra time scrutinizing each weight ticket.
Some claim to have no weight tickets because the amount hauled to a transfer station
was too minimal to be measured, leading to the improper disposal of C&D material that
could have been diverted from landfill. Projects taken on by repeat offenders vary in
size, illustrated by Figure 2, but the most problematic repeat offenders are
those with high-value projects that produce a significant amount of C&D material.

BACKGROUND
The City requires that all construction, demolition, and some remodel projects submit a
Construction Waste Management Plan (CWMP) that complies with its zero-waste
requirements (Berkeley Green Code BMC 19.37 and California Green Building
Standards Code Sections 4.408.2 and 5.408.1.1). Besides CWMP, all contractors are
required to upload C&D debris weight tickets to the Green Halo platform. These
weight tickets include information on the tons debris diverted from landfill and quantify
project materials which have been recycled or reused. Staff also host office hours at the
Permit Service Center on Tuesdays and Thursdays, allowing any contractors who are
having issues with Green Halo to consult with Zero Waste staff first-hand and address
their issues.

Zero Waste staff have been working on launching educational awareness campaigns to
further assist contractors lacking experience with the Green Halo platform, and
to encourage onboarding onto the Green Halo platform. Staff also conduct random site
inspections, to ensure that projects comply with state requirements, allowing for
interventions and flexibility when necessary. Additionally, Zero Waste staff participate in
Design-Stage Round Table reviews, and Field Inspection Project Kickoff meetings, to
provide notice of projects’ Berkeley Green Code (BMC 19.37) requirements.

Penalizing repeat offenders for non-compliance will level the playing field
and encourage development by contractors acting in good faith. The 65% diversion
requirement is already embedded in the Berkeley Green Code and applies to most
permitted construction and demolition projects in the City. Therefore, enforcing
the requirement should not materially slow development or reduce project feasibility.

On June 19, 2025, the Zero Waste Commission authorized its Green Building
Subcommittee to write and submit this referral to the City Council to request the City
Manager refer the Zero Waste Division of the Public Works Department, and the
Building and Safety Division, Energy and Sustainability and Green Building Program
Management staff from the Planning Department to research and recommend best
practices to codify enforcement mechanisms for improving compliance with state and
city-mandated C&D debris diversion requirements.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Lack of effective diversion can be damaging to local communities. The construction
industry is considered to be the primary contributor to landfill material; in the United
States, 67% of all solid waste is generated by the C&D industry alone (Chen et al.,
2021). C&D debris is also the primary cause of environmental pollution; debris that ends
up in landfill contains inorganics, heavy metals, organics, pesticides, and oils that leach
into the landscape and contaminate soil and groundwater (Chen et al., 2021). Improper
C&D debris salvaging also leads to indirect environmental damage, such as
consumption of usable land, energy and non-energy resource consumption, resource
depletion, air pollution, noise pollution, water pollution, and more (Chen et al., 2021).

Inadequate diversion introduces health-harming pollutants to the environment, as wind
carries particles from landfills into neighboring communities. As landfills expand,
substances like silica, asbestos, heavy metals, and volatile organic compounds can
become airborne, and expose particularly low-income populations to respiratory
irritants, allergens, and carcinogens (Dorevitch et al., 2006). This is especially alarming,
as studies show that higher percentages of Black and Hispanic residents, as well as
households with lower socioeconomic status, are in close proximity to landfills (Joseph
and Kamanmalek, 2025).

Successful C&D diversion can yield results that are beneficial to surrounding
communities. A study by the EPA found that diverting 70-90% of debris can reduce 250-
400 kg of CO2 per ton of material, improving air quality in the area (Shajidha,
and Mortula, 2025). In India, the recycling of C&D debris was found to improve all 15
impact categories of the recycling life cycle assessment, with observations like
decreased leachate improving soil and groundwater, lower contamination from heavy
metals, and reduced habitat disruption (Ram et al., 2020). Effective enforcement of C&D
diversion is necessary if Berkeley is to sustain healthy communities and mitigate the
harmful effects of climate change.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Establishing an effective enforcement mechanism will support staff in bringing repeat
offenders into compliance, levelling the playing field for all contractors and encouraging
contractors who work in good faith. Beyond informing contractors of their responsibilities
to meet the 65% diversion minimum, staff currently have little power to hold contractors
accountable, especially those that are repeatedly out of compliance, and repeatedly act
in bad faith.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The alternative is no action as it relates to enforcement. Staff continue increasing
outreach and education measures which only address part of the non-compliance issue




                                                                                  Page 318
                                         Page 7 of 7

Enforceable Mechanism for Berkeley Green Code Compliance         CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                      October 27, 2026




and do not target those bad actors who have repeatedly been out of compliance for the
past decade with no consequence.

The City originally adopted the Berkeley Green Code Chapter 19.37 on November 29,
2016, and the code went into effect on January 1, 2017. This adoption mandated 65-
percent diversion of construction and demolition materials and 100-percent diversion of
excavated soil, concrete, and asphalt. However, the Berkeley Municipal Code does not
include a clear pathway to enforcing the waste diversion requirements. As a result, staff
must rely on contractor self-reporting, which has led to noncompliance, including
improper source separation, fraudulent, missing or late weight ticket uploads, and
repeated violations by the same contractors.

Currently, the City requires all construction, demolition, and remodeling projects to
submit a Construction Waste Management Plan and upload construction and demolition
debris weight tickets to Green Halo, a cloud-based software platform. This platform is
used by staff for waste tracking and approval or denial of submitted weight tickets that
document compliance with the statewide 65-percent construction and demolition
recycling requirement and the City’s 100-percent recycling requirements for asphalt,
cement and concrete. Public Works staff also provide technical assistance through
office hours, educational outreach, site inspections, and early project reviews.

In 2025, 17-percent of contractors remained out of compliance with the Berkeley Green
Code’s construction and demolition debris diversion requirements. There is no current
enforcement procedure within the Berkeley Green Code; this limits staff’s ability to hold
violators accountable. Actionable enforcement is essential for reducing landfill waste,
cutting greenhouse gas emissions, protecting frontline communities, and advancing the
City’s climate and equity goals.

Mixed and improperly bagged debris, miscoded tickets, and unverifiable data
further undermine diversion outcomes and staff oversight. Staff have identified
forty (40) repeat offenders who have been out of compliance for over a decade.
Repeat offenders pose the greatest challenge, particularly on high-value projects
that generate large volumes of waste. Establishing a clear enforcement
mechanism is a necessary next step to ensure compliance with state and local
requirements, reduce the administrative burden on City staff who request
information from non-responsive or uncooperative permittees, and to ensure that




                                                                                       Page 3233
                                             Page 4 of 5

Companion Report: Enforceable Mechanism for Berkeley Green Code Compliance   CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                                 October 27, 2026




permits are not finalized until the City receives all of the requested compliance
documentation.

Staff cannot enforce mandated construction and demolition debris diversion
requirements because there is currently no enforcement mechanism in the Berkeley
Municipal Code. This gap in the municipal code creates ongoing challenges with
compliance. Amending the code to allow for enforcement of CALGreen requirements
will not materially slow development or reduce project feasibility. The 65-percent
diversion requirement is already embedded in the Berkeley Green Code and applies to
most permitted construction and demolition projects in Berkeley.

Developing a recommendation for the City Council to adopt enforcement
mechanisms to strengthen compliance with California Green Building Standards
Code advances the Strategic Plan goal to be a global leader in addressing
climate change, advancing environmental justice, and protecting the
environment. To wit, construction and demolition waste diversion is critical to
reducing landfill use, greenhouse gas emissions, and environmental
degradation.

BACKGROUND
CALGreen 4.408.2 and 5.408.1.1 are part of the California Green Building Standards
Code’s construction waste management provisions, specifically for Universal Waste.

4.408.2 – Universal Waste Management

       Applies to certain projects where Universal Waste is generated during
        construction or demolition.

       Requires verification that Universal Waste is managed correctly in accordance
        with applicable state and local regulations.

       A list of prohibited Universal Waste materials must be included in the project’s
        construction documents.

       This is a mandatory compliance method for those projects that produce
        Universal Waste, ensuring it is not disposed of in a way that violates
        environmental regulations.

5.408.1.1 – Construction Waste Management Plan

       Applies when the project meets the C&D waste diversion threshold (≥ 65-
        percent diversion or ≤2 lbs./ft² disposal for nonresidential; lower limits for
        residential) but must submit a Construction Waste Management Plan (CWMP).



                                                                                       Page 3244
                                             Page 5 of 5

Companion Report: Enforceable Mechanism for Berkeley Green Code Compliance   CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                                 October 27, 2026




The CWMP must:

           Outline the waste diversion and recycling strategy.

           Identify the methods and facilities used for diversion/recycling.

           Include a schedule for waste handling and disposal.

           Be updated as necessary during construction and accessible to the
            enforcing agency for inspection

Berkeley Green Code diversion requirements were adopted in the Berkeley Municipal
Code as Chapter 19.37, requiring 65-percent of construction and demolition material be
diverted from landfill, and 100-percent of excavated soil, concrete, and asphalt.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Effective enforcement of construction and demolition debris diversion is critical to
reducing landfill use, cutting greenhouse gas emissions, protecting air and water quality,
and preventing disproportionate health and environmental harms to low-income and
minority communities, while supporting Berkeley’s climate and environmental
sustainability goals.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Compliance challenges with construction and demolition debris diversion requirements
primarily result from the absence of a clear path for the City to enforce the
requirements. This limits staff’s ability to hold contractors, particularly repeat and bad-
faith offenders, accountable and underscores the need for a clear enforcement
framework to support effective compliance.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The alternative action to the proposed recommendation would be taking no action.

RECOMMENDATION
Recommend that Council refer the matter to the City Manager with direction to:

      1. Instruct the Zero Waste Division, in collaboration with the Planning
         Department and Fire Department, to study, research, and recommend policies
         that standardize requirements for:

            a. Tenant-facing materials collection rooms for refuse, dual-stream recycling,
               and composting

            b. Central collection rooms or enclosures

            c. Curbside collection staging areas for all new construction

      2. Develop minimum per-unit service requirements, design parameters, and
         enforcement mechanisms; pursuant to Chapter 12.32.030 and 12.35 of the

SUMMARY
While the Berkeley Municipal Code mandates accessible waste storage, it fails to
outline efficient refuse, dual-stream recycling and compost collection areas for tenants
and employees, central collection locations or safe curbside staging areas for
collection and enforce proper space allocation for said collection processes in the
design phase of project lifecycles. Improper space allocation for refuse, dual-stream
recycling and compost carts and bins in new commercial construction blueprints
increases construction costs while compromising Zero Waste collection services and
the safety of City workers.

There is an opportunity to codify refuse collection procedures and facilitate compliance
by enforcing proper space allocation across all new commercial developments. In this
effort, areas for focused research include, but are not limited to, the development of:

                                                                         October 27, 2026




   1. Minimum service requirements. Minimum service requirements create a baseline
      expectancy for refuse volume across all new commercial construction, allowing
      for the development of baseline design guidelines and a standardization of space
      allocation in refuse collection procedures.

   2. Design parameters. In order to streamline refuse, dual-stream recycling and
      compost collection in new construction projects, design guidelines
      that allocate sufficient space to accommodate required collection services in
      every stage of the collection process are necessary.

   3. Enforcement mechanisms. Ensuring adherence to a standardized refuse
      collection procedure ensures the safety, health, and cleanliness of the city.

Staff in the Zero Waste Division of the Public Works Department, in conjunction with the

policies, including the potential for cost-recovery through bill back for staff time and
enforcement mechanisms. Assessment of these fiscal impacts will require minimal staff
time.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Under Chapter 12.32.030 of the Berkeley Municipal Code, the City of Berkeley requires
“[every] person owning any premises, where garbage or rubbish is produced or
accumulated [is to] provide and maintain…in a suitable place readily accessible to
personnel of the solid waste and environmental health divisions, containers of sufficient
capacity and number to store the accumulations of garbage or rubbish during the
intervals between collections or disposal”. Under Chapter 12.35.010 of the Berkeley
Municipal Code, the City of Berkeley adopted and codified the Short-Lived Climate
Pollutants Organic Waste Reduction Strategy “The purpose of this Ordinance is to
comply with certain state laws requiring cities, counties, and special districts providing
solid waste collection services to adopt ordinances and take other measures to reduce
the amount of organic and recyclable materials deposited in landfills from commercial
and residential generators, more specifically the Short-Lived Climate Pollutants Organic
Waste Reduction regulations adopted pursuant to Senate Bill 1383 (Statutes of 2016)
set forth in the California Code of Regulations (the "SB 1383 Regulations"). Notably, the
requirements not only emphasize the importance of establishing sufficient space for
waste collection, but also mandate that containers of collected refuse are “readily
accessible to personnel”.

The City of Berkeley operates municipal refuse collection in two ways:

   1. Curbside Service. Building owners are responsible for placing refuse, dual
      stream recycling, and compost carts or bins at the appropriate staging locations
      along the street prior to collection day, and returning them to their enclosures
      within 24 hours.



                                                                                Page 328
                                           Page 3 of 7

Research on Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance       CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                           October 27, 2026




   2. Push-and-Pull Service: Building owners pay the City an additional fee to
      transport carts and bins from a central collection area to a curbside collection
      area and back.

The mandated collection process consists of the following three stages:

   1. Occupant Refuse, Dual-Stream Recycling and Compost Collection. The first
      stage covers occupant access to material collection containers, at either a central
      collection location or in the case of large multi-family buildings, material collection
      rooms on each floor. In accordance with the BMC, equal access to all waste
      streams must be ensured across all building levels.

   2. Staging. This stage covers the process of transporting collected materials to their
      proper staging area for collection. Important technicalities in this stage include,
      but are not limited to: doorway dimensions, alley widths, and slope gradients.

   3. Municipal Refuse Collection. The final stage covers the municipal collection of
      the material from curbside staging areas for transportation to the Transfer
      Station. Important technicalities in this stage include, but are not limited to: curb
      cuts, red or yellow zones for ease of collection truck parking, considerations to
      avoid bike lanes and staging areas on busy thoroughfares, driveway, approach,
      and slope gradient.

Although the Zero Waste Division has published New Construction: Adequate Space
Guidelines for Waste Containers and provides developers with a copy of these
guidelines, the City’s refuse, dual-stream recycling and compost collection process, as
well as the aforementioned space guidelines, are not codified in the Berkeley Municipal
Code, rendering enforcement impossible for City staff.

Unfortunately, the consequence of a lack of formalized specifications for new
construction design and no enforceable mechanisms for ensuring space is properly
allocated for tenant facing trash rooms, central collection rooms or enclosures and
proper staging areas that take into account driver and pedestrian safety, staff encounter
completed new construction that has failed to accommodate at least one stage of refuse
collection, including but not limited to:

   o   Doors to refuse enclosures with insufficient clearance to accommodate bin
       collection services requested by the property, necessitating design modifications

   o   Dumpsters are placed in narrow alleyways. Enclosures and storage areas must
       have enough space for dumpsters. If moving a dumpster, ensure a curb cut
       is installed for push-pull service.

   o   Steeply sloped driveways from enclosures to the street, resulting in staff injuries
       during push-and-pull service provision;



                                                                                  Page 329
                                           Page 4 of 7

Research on Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance      CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




   o   Alleyways with insufficient vertical clearance for refuse truck entrance;

   o   Trash chutes with no collocated chutes for recycling or compost;

   o   Staging locations that impede biker and pedestrian right-of-way;

   o   Negligent staging that leads to increased street litter from upended bins.

These issues not only compromise proper waste separation but can result in costly
post-construction design modifications. Furthermore, inefficiencies place unnecessary
administrative burden on staff, while endangering Zero Waste materials collection
workers. In order to streamline refuse collection procedures and
prevent aforementioned issues, important design elements that will be considered,
categorized under each stage, include but will not be limited to:

   1. Occupant Refuse Collection: equal access to all waste streams across all
      building levels, in accordance with BMC 12.35.

   2. Staging: Maintain a minimum 18-inch clearance between dumpsters staged side
      by side. This required clearance would greatly reduce pinch hazards and prevent
      hand injuries during handling.

   3. Doorway Dimensions: Entrances must provide enough width for containers plus
      6 inches on either side to pass through freely without hitting frames. This
      prevents property damage and ensures smooth transitions between spaces.

   4. Alley Widths: Driveways and alleys must be wide enough to allow for safe
      maneuvering of both containers and collection vehicles. Adequate space is
      essential to avoid scraping walls or damaging property.

   5. Gradients: Gradients of staging areas will be considered and addressed
      to ensure reduce runaway dumpster hazard does not occur. Steep inclines are
      prohibited as they significantly increase the risk of injuries and property damage.

   6. Surface & Obstructions: Containers must be kept on a smooth, level surface free
      of any debris or obstacles to reduce physical strain to our staff and reduce tipping
      accidents or injuries.

   7. Public Right-of-Way: Containers and equipment must be positioned so they do
      not obstruct the public right-of-way or traffic lanes to increase safety of both the
      collection crew and the general public.

Proper space allocation for refuse collection, which includes instituting minimum service
requirements and creating pre-construction design guidelines, is a crucial next step for
streamlining compliance with materials collection and waste disposal requirements.




                                                                                   Page 330
                                           Page 5 of 7

Research on Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance      CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




Staff expect that codifying the space allocation requirement will not materially slow
development or reduce project feasibility. The guidelines are already
informally required and codifying them will offer the opportunity to include an
enforcement mechanism and increase compliance with BMC 12.35.

BACKGROUND
All commercial and multi-family (5+ units) properties within the City of Berkeley are
subject to State Law SB 1383 and corresponding local Alameda County Organics
Reduction and Recycling Ordinance (2021-02). In order to be in compliance with SB
1383, the City of Berkeley must accommodate four waste streams through materials
collection procedures:

   1. Landfill,
   2. Recycling for Glass, Metals, and Plastics,
   3. Recycling for Cardboard, Mixed Paper, and
   4. Organics collection for Food Waste, Compostable Paper, and Plant Debris.

From 2019 to 2023, the Telegraph Business Improvement District and Downtown
Berkeley Association piloted trash corrals— structures designed to contain businesses’
waste bins on the street— in order to “make trash collection easier, and provide a more
pleasing streetscape1.” Part of an early effort to introduce trash enclosures by
commercial districts, this pilot project exemplifies the need for allocating space for waste
receptacles, given the implications of uncorralled receptacles in the public right of way.

At its meeting September 18, 2025, the Zero Waste Commission authorized its Green
Building Subcommittee to write and submit this referral to the City Council to authorize
the City Manager to refer the Public Works Zero Waste Division, to work in conjunction
with the Planning Department to study, research and recommend procedures and
enforcement mechanisms to increase proper waste sorting compliance by ensuring all
new commercial construction includes the proper allocation of space to accommodate
state and city-mandated waste collection requirements.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Compromised refuse collection processes frequently expose waste to the environment
and its natural processes, adversely impacting environmental health. Improperly staged



                                                                                 Page 331
                                           Page 6 of 7

Research on Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance      CONSENT CALENDAR
                                                                          October 27, 2026




refuse bins are subject to being knocked over or left uncovered, and rainwater runoff
from unenclosed waste creates leachate containing microplastics such as polyethylene,
polystyrene, and polypropylene2. As leachate enters Berkeley’s stormwater drainage
systems, these microplastics inevitably contaminate the Bay. Clogged drainpipes are a
consequential causative factor of water logging in urban areas3, thus unenclosed
waste and litter that result in clogged storm drains increase flood risks amidst already
intensifying storms. Furthermore, 80% of global marine litter originates from land4. The
City of Berkeley’s contribution to this number could be significantly reduced
by establishing effective refuse collection policies and processes. Beyond these
impacts, inadequate materials collection infrastructure in multifamily developments
significantly limits resident and business participation in proper refuse, recycling, and
composting. When collection areas are inconvenient or poorly designed, participation
declines, contamination increases, and diversion goals are undermined. Improving
access and usability of tenant-facing collection spaces is therefore critical to increasing
participation and achieving environmental outcomes.

Successful allocation of waste receptacles can benefit all local communities. Proper
management is projected to conserve resources, reduce greenhouse gas emissions,
save energy, and decrease pollutants5. Studies have shown that proper programs for
waste management not only reduce environmental harm but improve the physical and
mental health of citizens6.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The absence of code requirements on space allocation for efficient material collection
and enforcement of minimum service requirements in the City of Berkeley, has
restricted staff’s ability to enforce compliance with our recommendations for proper
space allocation in the pre-design and construction phases of the project lifecycle. This
has led to development of properties that complicate the material collection process,
elevating health and environmental risks. Problems at all levels of the refuse collection
process occur without explicit standards for appropriate space allocation, and a lack of
enforcement allows for these conditions to persist.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The alternative action to the proposed recommendation would be taking no action.

See companion report.

To:                Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
From:              Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
Submitted by: Jamie Parks, Director, Public Works
Subject:           Companion Report: Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance
                   with Source Separated Refuse Collection Procedures

RECOMMENDATION
Adopt first reading of an ordinance amending Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 12.32 –
Storage, Collection and Disposal of Waste.

SUMMARY
New commercial developments in Berkeley must have adequate space for refuse,
recycling, and compost collection. The Public Works, Planning and Fire departments
developed proposed amendments to the Berkeley Municipal Code to set safe and
commonsense requirements for source separated refuse collection. The Zero Waste
Commission’s report reinforces work that staff are currently undertaking. The intentions
of these requirements are to improve and increase waste sorting and, thus, reduce
spills, contamination, greenhouse gas emissions from landfills, and other environmental,
health and safety harms.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
Public Works’ Zero Waste Division, the Planning Department’s Building and Safety
Division and Energy, Sustainability and Green Building Program Management groups,
and the Fire Department have already implemented a workflow that addresses the
requirements put forth in the Zero Waste Commission’s proposed ordinance language.
Therefore, no additional staffing time or associated costs are anticipated.

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
Public Works staff recommend Council adopt the first reading of an ordinance to amend
Chapter 12.32 of the Berkeley Municipal Code to add Section 12.32.035 (“Adequate
Space for Collection Containers”), which will clarify requirements for commercial
developments to provide for the convenient sorting of refuse into landfill, recycling and
compost streams and to require the construction of central collection locations or trash
enclosures that are safe and easily accessible for Public Works staff to collect. Staff
expect that codifying the space allocation requirement will not materially slow
development or reduce project feasibility.



    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
                         E-Mail: manager@berkeleyca.gov Website: https://berkeleyca.gov/

Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 12.32.030 requires property owners to provide
adequate and accessible refuse materials collection space. This section of the code
does not describe what design standards should be considered. Additionally, there are
no clear minimum service guidelines used to estimate the amount of space needed for
“adequate collection space”. As a result, Public Works staff have worked closely with
Planning staff to ensure that new construction projects receive the necessary feedback
so that their construction plans comply with State, County and Local zero waste
requirements.

Public Works staff have encountered very few applicants who refuse to collaborate and,
therefore, do not anticipate a need to institute post-construction penalization. This
collaborative process has increased worker safety, environmental health and landfill
diversion. Additional design considerations in the municipal code will provide the
missing clarification that will provide additional support to continue the current success
and improve diversion efforts.

Amending Chapter 12.32 of the Berkeley Municipal Code to require adequate space for
collection containers advances the Strategic Plan goal to be a global leader in
addressing climate change, advancing environmental justice, and protecting the
environment.

BACKGROUND
The State of California's Senate Bill 1383 on Short-Lived Climate Pollutants requires
that all refuse generators, residents and businesses, subscribe to landfill, recycling and
organics collection services, provide equally accessible and convenient access to all of
the required streams and to provide proper signage to increase participation in proper
sorting and landfill diversion. These requirements are in line with the City’s zero waste
and climate action goals and were adopted into the municipal code under chapter 12.35
Organics Reduction and Recycling.

Public Works and Planning staff have built a strong relationship over the last three years
to implement an improved workflow where safety and compliance concerns are
discussed and addressed directly with new construction designers. Public Works staff
recognized that new buildings were being permitted without adequate space to
accommodate the City’s required four stream collection services. This led to reduced
participation in proper sorting and therefore, reduced opportunities to increase diversion
from landfill. It was also leading to Public Works collection drivers being exposed to
safety hazards related to refuse collection sites being placed in areas with pinch
hazards, steep slopes, access issues or public right of ways with heavy traffic.

The Zero Waste Commission Secretary reported on progress addressing this issue at
multiple Zero Waste Commission meetings beginning in September of 2023 to present,
the Zero Waste Commission voted to move a referral to Council on September 18,



                                                                                       Page 3362
                                               Page 3 of 25

Companion Report: Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance with   CONSENT CALENDAR
Source Separated Refuse Collection Procedures                                      October 27, 2026




2025, requesting that Council adopt an ordinance that would codify the informal process
staff had built to address its space allocation issue.

The amendments to Chapter 12.32 of the Municipal Code proposed by staff reflect a
significant modification to the to the amendments proposed by the Zero Waste
Commission with respect to residential development. The Zero Waste Commission's
recommendations contemplated application of the new waste storage, collection,
staging, and space-allocation requirements to multifamily residential development and
mixed-use development. Following further review by City staff, the proposed ordinance
has been revised to remove residential development, including the residential
component of mixed-use development, from the new physical space-allocation and
design requirements. Assembly Bill 130 (Stats. 2025, ch. 22) generally prohibits cities
and counties, from October 1, 2025 through June 1, 2031, from adopting new or more
restrictive building standards applicable to residential units unless a statutory exception
applies. The City can revisit residential developments after June 1, 2031.

Right now, the new Zero Waste space-allocation and design requirements cannot be
enforced against residential developments without conflicting with AB 130. Accordingly,
the proposed ordinance does not apply new physical design requirements to residential
development. Zero Waste requirements that do not establish new residential building
standards, like curbside waste collection procedures, are not affected by this
modification.

Certain proposed fire and life-safety amendments recommended by the Fire
Department will continue to apply to residential development. Many of these provisions
do not establish new building standards, but instead expressly require compliance with
existing requirements of the California Building Code, California Fire Code, Berkeley
Fire Code, and Berkeley Wildland-Urban Interface Code. These include requirements
governing waste and recycling chutes and associated shafts and collection rooms;
combustible waste storage and separation; fire apparatus and emergency access;
unobstructed access to fire hydrants, fire department connections, and other fire
protection equipment; means of egress; existing requirements governing battery
collection and storage; and applicable Wildland-Urban Interface requirements.




                                                                                       Page 3373
                                               Page 4 of 25

Companion Report: Proper Space Allocation for Standardizing Compliance with   CONSENT CALENDAR
Source Separated Refuse Collection Procedures                                      October 27, 2026




To the extent any Fire Department provision establishes a new or more restrictive
residential building standard beyond existing code requirements, the City intends to
seek approval under AB 130's health-and-safety exception. Health and Safety Code
sections 17958, 17958.5, and 17958.7 permit a local residential building standard
during the AB 130 moratorium where the California Building Standards Commission
determines that the change or modification is necessary as an emergency standard to
protect health and safety.

The Fire Department's proposed requirements most directly related to this exception are
those intended to preserve required fire apparatus and emergency access; prevent
obstruction of fire lanes, hydrants, fire department connections, means of egress, and
other fire protection equipment; regulate combustible waste and battery storage that
presents a fire hazard; and ensure that waste storage or staging facilities do not
interfere with required fire and life-safety features. If the California Building Standards
Commission does not approve a new residential standard under the applicable AB 130
exception, that standard would not be enforced against residential development during
the AB 130 moratorium.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
Improperly managed materials collection in Berkeley can reduce participation by
business tenants and employees in commercial buildings, resulting in missed
opportunities to divert recyclable and compostable materials from landfills. This
increases greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane from decomposing organic
waste. In addition, spillage from improperly contained waste can contribute to
microplastic contamination of waterways, increase flood risks, and add to marine litter.
Proper allocation and management of waste receptacles help reduce pollution,
conserve resources, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and improve community health
and safety.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
Making the City’s space allocation standards easier to understand and formally adding
them to the Berkeley Municipal Code will give engineers, architects, and contractors
clearer design requirements. It will also allow staff to point applicants to an official set of
rules before they submit their construction plans to Public Works for review.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
City Council could decide not to adopt a first reading of the proposed additional chapter
to the Berkeley Municipal Code. Taking no action would maintain the status quo, leaving
codified requirements vague and enforcement options unclear.

12.32.010       Definitions.

A. "Garbage" means putrescible animal or vegetable matter, and containers used for
the storage thereof. "Garbage" does not include source-separated recyclables or yard
waste.

B. "Hazardous waste" means that waste defined in Health and Safety Code Section
25117.

C. "Medical waste" means that waste defined in Health and Safety Code Section
25023.2

D. "Rubbish" means all nonputrescible waste matter, whether combustible or
noncombustible, except hazardous waste and medical waste.

E. "Waste" means the useless, unused, unwanted or discarded material resulting from
normal community activities, or materials which by their presence may injuriously affect
the health, safety and comfort of persons and depreciate property values in the vicinity
thereof. "Waste" shall include, but not be limited to garbage, putrescible organic
material, rubbish, offal, swill, animal excreta, rubble, plaster or other waste resulting
from the demolition, burning, alteration or construction of buildings or structures.

F. "Source-separated recyclables" means non-putrescible materials that are separated
by the generator from other waste material for the purpose of reuse or recycling, by
placing the recyclables in separate containers, or by binding them separately; the
recyclable material is then kept separate from general rubbish by the collector and
processor, and is returned to the economic mainstream in the form of raw material for
new, reused or reconstituted products which meet the quality standards necessary to be




                                                                                   Page 341
                                        Page 8 of 25




used in the marketplace. Source separated recyclables contain no more than 20% of
material which is disposed of as refuse by the collector or their subcontractors.

G. "Yard waste" means grass, weeds, leaves, tree trimmings, plants, shrubbery
prunings, and such other similar materials which are generated in the maintenance of
yards, gardens or landscaping, and which are separated by the generator from other
solid waste materials for the purpose of recycling or composting, and which are taken
by the hauler to a recycling or composting facility. (Ord. 6549-NS § 2, 2000; Ord. 6517-
NS § 2, 1999; Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)

H. “Central consolidation location” means internal area generally located on the first
floor or in the basement of a multi-story mixed use, commercial or multi-family
building that is of adequate size to house waste receptacles that meet minimum service
requirements including but not limited to landfill, dual-stream recycling and
organics where materials from tenants can be centrally consolidate for collection.

I. “Minimum service requirements” mean all property owners or property managers are
required to subscribe to landfill, dual-stream recycling and organics collection services
at a minimum of 20 gallons per unit to ensure adequate service is provided to
comply with state, county and local zero waste mandates. Waste enclosures or central
consolidation locations shall be designed to accommodate the collection receptacles to
meet minimum service requirements.

J. “Multi-family building” means property with five or more residential units.

K. “Mixed-use building” means multi-story property containing one or multiple
businesses on the first story(s) with residential housing units on additional stories.

L. Tenant Facing Collection Room: rooms located on each story of a multi-story mixed
use, commercial or multi-family building where tenants have convenient access to do
dispose of landfill, dual-stream recycling and organics. If utilizing trash chutes, there
must be enough chutes to accommodate all required material collection streams.

MJ. Staging Area: area where Public Works staff will collect landfill, dual-stream
recycling and organic materials for disposal or processing, generally located in the
public right of way, at the waste enclosure or at the central consolidation location and
shall not be located more than 100 ft from where the collection vehicle will need to park
to provide service. If located in the public right of way, curb cuts and red zones must be




                                                                                    Page 342
                                        Page 9 of 25




provided to ensure safe transport and storage of the collection receptacles on the day(s)
of service.

NK. Valet Waste Service: a third-party service that collects municipal solid waste from
outside of tenant's units and properly sorts it for disposal eliminating the need for tenant
facing trash rooms. If utilizing a valet waste service, ensure the service provider has
been adequately trained and approved by Public Works Department staff.

OL. Waste Enclosure: A stand-alone covered area on a commercial or multi-family
property designed to house receptacles for storing solid municipal waste including but
not limited to landfill, dual-stream recyclables, and organics.



C. “Universal waste” means universal waste as defined in the California Health and
Safety Code Section 25123.8 and California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5,
Chapter 23. Universal waste includes certain batteries, electronic waste, non-empty
aerosols cans, and other special materials designated as universal waste under
applicable state law and is subject to the applicable requirements governing its
collection, storage, handing, recycling, and disposal.



12.32.020     Accumulation prohibited--Storage requirements--Removal of
construction rubbish.

A. No person owning any multiple-family dwelling or possessing any single-family
dwelling, or industrial, commercial or business premises or structure shall allow or
permit any garbage, rubbish or waste to collect and accumulate upon or in any such
premises or structure except as otherwise provided by law. This provision shall not be
construed as affecting any authorized waste disposal operation or properly conducted
garden composting process carried on by a private individual in their own premises and
for their own use and done in a manner consistent with this section.

B. During intervals between collection or disposal, the storage, accumulation,
collection, keeping, handling or maintaining of waste on premises where produced shall
be performed in such a manner as to prevent the harboring and breeding of rodents,
insects and other vermin and as to prevent ready access to the waste by dogs and
other small animals; as to prevent objectionable odors in the ambient air; as not to
constitute a fire hazard; and as not to result in such unsightliness as to result in the



                                                                                   Page 343
                                       Page 10 of 25




depreciation of the value of adjacent property or the comfortable enjoyment of life
thereon.

C. Construction and Demolition Rubbish and Waste. During construction, alteration,
or demolition activities, combustible debris, rubbish, and waste materials shall be
managed in accordance with California Fire Code Section 3304, as applicable.
Combustible debris, rubbish, and waste materials shall not be accumulated within
buildings and shall be removed from buildings at the end of each shift of work.

   1. Temporary rubbish containers exceeding 5.33 cubic feet (40 gallons) used for
       combustible debris, rubbish, or waste shall be provided with tight-fitting or self-
       closing lids and shall be constructed of noncombustible materials or other
       materials complying with California Fire Code Section 3304.1.3.

   2. Materials susceptible to spontaneous ignition, including oily rags, shall be stored
       in listed disposal containers in accordance with California Fire Code Section
       3304.2.

   3. Construction and demolition waste containers shall not be located or maintained
       so as to obstruct required fire apparatus access, means of egress, fire hydrants,
       fire department connections, or access to required fire protection equipment.

C. Every person, contractor or builder engaged in the construction, repair or
demolition of any building or structure shall at reasonable intervals dispose of or remove
from such premises all rubbish resulting from the construction, repair or demolition and
within a reasonable time of the final cessation of work on such building, structure or
premises. (Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)




12.32.030        Garbage containers required--Specifications--Use restrictions--
                 Location.

A. Every person owning any premises, where garbage or rubbish is produced or
accumulated shall provide and maintain on the premises in a suitable place readily
accessible to personnel of the solid waste and environmental health divisions,
containers of sufficient capacity and number to store the accumulations of garbage or




                                                                                   Page 344
                                       Page 11 of 25




rubbish during the intervals between collections or disposal. With the written of the
owner, nonresidential tenants may contract for garbage collection service
independently, either on their own behalf or on the owner’s behalf, if the owner agrees
in writing to guaranty payment of the garbage collection charge in the event the tenant
does not pay it in a timely fashion.

B. Every contractor or builder engaged in the erection or repair of a building shall
provide sufficient containers at or near such building for the deposit and storage of any
waste resulting from the erection or repair work.

C. Garbage containers for other than bulk accumulation shall be constructed of metal
or other impervious material approved by the managers of environmental health and
solid waste with tight-fitting covers. The containers and covers shall be in good repair,
leakproof, free from holes, flytight and rodentproof. Containers shall be equipped with
handles adequate to lift the weight of a full container without breaking or bending. Such
container shall be maintained in a sanitary condition by the owners thereof and covers
shall not be removed except for the purpose of placing waste therein or removing waste
therefrom.

D. Rubbish except broken glass, rocks, concrete, bricks and similar solid material,
plaster or dirt may be deposited in garbage containers. Hazardous waste, human waste
and other potentially infectious material shall not be deposited or placed in garbage
containers. Liquid garbage shall not be deposited or placed in such containers.

E. No garbage containers or other containers for waste, other than those of the City,
shall be placed, kept, stored or located within the right-of-way of a street or alley;
provided, however, that the Public Works Department may authorize the location of
such containers within the public right-of-way at specified places and times when such
location is necessary for the expeditious collection and disposition of garbage by the
City. (Ord. 6369-NS § 1 (part), 1997; Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)




12.32.04035      Findings and Purpose Findings and Purpose
A. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, refuse collection is one of the most fatal
civilian occupational activities. Furthermore, handling refuse is one of the greatest
sources of occupational injury for building maintenance staff. When refuse collection




                                                                                   Page 345
                                       Page 12 of 25




space is designated to an area that is difficult or unsafe to access by refuse collection
workers or custodial staff, it could cause serious injury or even death.

B. When sufficient space is not allocated for appropriate refuse collection receptacles,
including but not limited to landfill, dual-stream recycling and organics equally
conveniently located with appropriate capacities to contain all materials generated
onsite, the resulting building operational costs are often higher. If the space for refuse
collection receptacles is not designed properly, it may require additional sorting time on
the part of building staff or zero waste facilitators, require more frequent pickups by
haulers or result in extra haulers charges for refuse collection workers to move bins for
truck access, and may cause the building to incur charges, fines, or liens due to lack of
compliance with Berkeley’s zero waste service requirements.

C. Good design makes it easy to keep discarded materials separated for dual-
stream recycling, composting and landfill. When sufficient space is allocated for
all required streams in an equally convenient manner, materials will be more likely to be
sorted into the correct receptacle. When space for dual-stream recycling
and organics is an afterthought and designated to a less accessible or inconvenient
location, occupants and operators will be less likely to participate successfully in
recycling and organics collection programs.

DA. The purpose of this section is to ensure that new commercial development and
substantial renovations provide adequate space for the storage, collection, and
processing of solid waste, dual- stream recyclable, and organic materials or
construction and demolition materials in a manner that supports public health,
operational efficiency, compliance with state and local law, and the City's Zero Waste
and climate goals.




12.32.0540 Bulk wastes--Over one cubic yard--Over two cubic yards.

A. In any premises where a volume of waste in excess of one cubic yard is allowed to
accumulate between intervals of collection or disposal, such waste shall be managed in
the manner specified by the manager of the environmental health division for the
sanitary storage, collection or disposal of such waste on the premises.




                                                                                    Page 346
                                        Page 13 of 25




B. In addition to the requirements of subsection A of this section, dumpsters and
containers used for the storage of combustible waste shall comply with California Fire
Code Sections 304.3 through 304.3.7, as applicable, including requirements for
container construction, lids, location, separation from buildings, and fire protection.
Waste storage locations shall not create a fire hazard and shall be subject to approval
by the Fire Chief or designee where required by the California Fire Code. In addition to
the requirements of subsection A of this section, in any premises where a volume of
waste in excess of two cubic yards is allowed to accumulate between intervals of
collection or disposal, such waste shall be stored in fire-resistant containers and at
locations approved by the Fire Chief. (Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)

12.32.0650 Garbage collection--Service declared essential--Exclusive collection
by City required--Notification by owner--Fees--Time--Districts established--
Rubbish collected with garbage.


A. It is found and determined that the periodic collection of garbage from all premises
and places in the City in or from which garbage is created, accumulated or produced is
essential for the maintenance of the public health and welfare of the City and that the
provision by the City of such garbage collection service is a direct benefit to all premises
and places in or from which garbage is created, accumulated or produced to the owners
thereof.

B. Garbage collection service is provided by the City, and all owners of premises and
places in the City in or from which garbage is created, accumulated or produced shall
use or cause to be used, and pay the fees charged for, the City’s collection service. It is
unlawful for any person, other than authorized agents or employees of the City, to
collect, remove or dispose of garbage in the City; provided, however, that nothing
contained herein shall prevent the use of garbage disposal devices as provided in the
City plumbing code.

C. All owners of premises and places in or from which garbage is created,
accumulated or produced shall notify the solid waste division of the services department
of the City that collection of garbage from such premises or place is required and the
frequency of the collection required.

D. Fees for the collection of garbage shall be established by resolution of the City
Council. All owners of premises and places in the City from which garbage is collected,




                                                                                  Page 347
                                        Page 14 of 25




or the person with responsibility for those premises, shall pay the garbage collection
fees established by the City Council. In the event of nonpayment of the garbage
collection fees, the City, at its option, may discontinue furnishing garbage collection
service as set forth in Section 12.32.060, such discontinuance of service to be in
addition to any remedies that are available to the City to enforce payment of any unpaid
garbage collection fees.

E. Collection of garbage shall be made at least once a week from private residences
and as many times per week as the Director of Public Works may order from all other
places.

F. The Director of Public Works may establish districts in the City for the purpose of
collecting garbage and rubbish.

G. The City will collect and dispose of all rubbish which is deposited in garbage
containers as authorized in Section 12.32.030, and to the extent that equipment and
personnel are available as determined by the Director of Public Works, the City may
collect and dispose of rubbish other than that deposited in garbage containers, provided
such rubbish is placed in separate containers approved by the Director of Public Works
and provided further that such rubbish is of such size that it can be placed in such
separate containers. (Ord. 6369-NS § 1 (part), 1997; Ord. 6340-NS § 1 (part), 1996;
Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)




12.32.0760      Garbage fees--Payment requirements--Service charges.

A. Fees for garbage and rubbish collection shall be billed and paid periodically as
determined by the City. Any fee which is not paid in full on the thirty first day after billing
is delinquent, except that fees which are billed semiannually shall be deemed
delinquent on December 11th and April 11th. A penalty of ten percent shall be assessed
on any delinquent amount. Delinquent amounts greater than one year delinquent shall
accrue interest at the rate of one and one-half percent per month. Service on unpaid
accounts may be reduced or discontinued thirty days after mailing notice of
delinquency.

B. The City may elect to bill for garbage and rubbish collection service as a special
assessment on the property taxes and charges collected by the county with property




                                                                                     Page 348
                                      Page 15 of 25




taxes. The City may also elect to bill individual persons or businesses for service
provided directly to those persons or businesses; however, because the provision by
the City of garbage collection service is necessary for the public health and a benefit to
the public, and necessary to prevent the creation of public nuisances, any amounts
billed to persons or businesses are an obligation of both the user of the property who
generates the garbage and the owner of the property who benefits from its use by
others, and therefore also payable by, and debts of, the owner of the property.

C. The City may employ any method provided by state law for collection of service
fees, delinquent amounts, penalties and interest, and all remedies shall be cumulative.

D. No refunds will be made for decreases in service during the billing period in which
the decrease occurred.

E. The City may require payment of a deposit in the amount three times the monthly
service charge for any City garbage collection service ordered in any case where the
owner of the affected property is not ordering the service or the City is legally unable to
impose a lien on the property in the event the service charges are not paid by the
person or business ordering the service. Such deposits may be credited by the City
against an account after one year for residential accounts and two years for non-
residential accounts, if there have been no delinquencies during the applicable period.
In the event an account is closed while the City has custody of a deposit, the City shall
credit the amount of the deposit against the closing bill and refund any amount
remaining. (Ord. 6393-NS § 1, 1997; Ord. 6369-NS § 1 (part), 1997; Ord. 6340-NS § 1
(part), 1996; Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)

12.32.09065 Design Standards

A. Waste storage and collection areas shall:

   1. Provide adequate space for collection containers and related infrastructure
      sufficient to accommodate all required material streams and meet minimum
      service requirements including but not limited to:

          a. Landfill disposal.

          b. Recycling of paper and cardboard.

          c. Recycling of glass, metal, and plastic containers.

          d. Organic materials, including food scraps, compostable paper, and plant
             debris.

   2. Be designed to accommodate the size, number, and configuration of containers
      required for collection service.

   3. Provide convenient and equal access to all required material streams.

   4. Have signage identifying the types of materials corresponding to each respective
      waste stream. Signage shall be permanently posted on or painted onto each
      receptacle. General instructions about how to recycle shall be posted on the
      walls inside the enclosure. The name and phone number of the person
      responsible for maintenance of the enclosure shall be included on the sign with
      general instructions.

   5. Provide adequate access for commercial tenants, property owners and
      managers, facilities staff, third party valet waste service providers or Zero Waste
      collection staff.

   6. Provide sufficient maneuvering area to safely move containers between storage
      and collection locations.

   7. Include pathways, ramps, and access routes that meet applicable accessibility
      and safety requirements.




                                                                                Page 350
                                     Page 17 of 25




   8. Reduce incidents of significant slopes

   8. Maintain adequate vertical clearance for opening lids and servicing containers.

   9. Include sufficient staging space to support collection operations.

   10. “Waste storage, collection and staging areas shall be located or constructed in a
      manner not to obstruct or reduce required fire apparatus access roads, fire lanes,
      emergency access, means of egress, fire hydrants, fire department connections,
      or access to other required fire protection equipment.” Be located and designed
      to minimize conflicts with vehicle circulation, pedestrian access, and emergency
      access requirements.

   11. Be maintained in a manner that supports cleanliness, safety, and proper
      collection operations.

B. Fire Protection and Life Safety Requirements.

Waste storage areas, rooms, enclosures, and associated waste containers shall comply
with the following Fire and Life Safety Requirements:

   1. Fire Protection. Waste storage areas, rooms, enclosures, and associated waste
      containers shall comply with California Fire Code (CFC) Sections 304.3.1
      through 304.3.7, including applicable requirements for location, construction, and
      separation. Where automatic sprinkler protection is utilized or other an approved
      method of compliance, such protection shall be provided in accordance with the
      applicable provisions of the CFC and applicable National Fire Protection
      Association (NFPA) standard.

   2. Battery Collection and Storage. Where waste storage areas, collection rooms,
      enclosures, or other collection facilities are used for the collection or storage of
      lithium-ion, lithium-metal, or other batteries, such collection and storage shall
      comply with CFC Section 320. Damaged, defective, recalled, leaking, swollen, or
      other compromised batteries shall be handled and stored in accordance with the
      CFC and hazardous material requirements.

   3. Battery-Powered Equipment and Charging. Waste storage areas, collection
      rooms, and waste enclosures shall not be used for the charging of powered
      micromobility devices or other battery-powered equipment unless specifically
      approved and permitted by the CFC, including Section 322.

   4. Emerging and Special Fire Hazards. The collection, storage, handling, or
      processing of materials presenting special or emerging fire hazards, including
      lithium-ion, lithium-metal, or other battery technology shall comply with the



                                                                                Page 351
                                  Page 18 of 25




   applicable provisions of the CFC and BFC. Where required by the CFC, such
   operations shall be subject to review and approval by the Fire Chief or designee.

5. Use of Waste Storage Areas and Enclosures. Waste storage areas, rooms,
   enclosures, and associated containers shall be used and maintained for their
   approved purpose. Containers shall not be filled beyond their designated
   capacity and, where lids are required, shall be maintained so that lids can fully
   close. Waste or other combustible materials shall not be allowed to accumulate
   outside designated containers or in a manner that creates a fire hazard, obstructs
   required means of egress, or obstructs or impairs required Fire Department
   access or access to fire protection equipment.

      a. Combustible storage, hazardous and universal waste or hazardous
         materials shall not be stored within exit passageways, interior exit
         enclosures or stairways, under unenclosed exterior exit or exit access
         stairways.

6. Fire Department Access. Waste storage, collection, and staging areas shall be
   located and maintained so as not to obstruct, reduce, or otherwise interfere with
   required fire apparatus access roads, fire lanes, emergency access to building
   exterior doors, openings and roofs required by the California Building Code,
   California Residential Code and California Fire Code, means of egress, fire
   hydrants, fire sprinkler system risers, fire department connections, or access to
   required fire protection system equipment in accordance with applicable
   provisions of the CFC Sections 503, 504, 507, 509, and 912.

      a. To ensure and maintain compliance, all developments requiring
         centralized waste, recycling, and/or organic collection shall construct
         dedicated concrete staging enclaves or recessed storage cutouts. These
         staging infrastructure elements must be situated entirely outside of the
         minimum required unobstructed width and vertical clearance of any
         designated fire apparatus access road, preventing any temporary or
         permanent container encroachment during stating or servicing.

7. Wildland-Urban Interface and Fire Hazard Areas. Where a project is located
   within an area subject to applicable Berkeley wildland-urban interface, fire hazard
   severity zone, defensible space, or vegetation management requirements,
   exterior waste storage areas and enclosures shall be designed, located and
   constructed of noncombustible materials in accordance with the applicable
   Berkeley Fire Code (BFC) and other adopted fire-safety requirements. [Berkeley
   Municipal Code Chapter 19.49]

8. Maintenance of Fire and Life Safety Features. Waste containers, storage
   areas, collection rooms, enclosures, and staging areas shall be maintained so as
   not to obstruct or reduce required fire apparatus access, emergency access,
   means of egress, fire hydrants, fire department connections, fire protection




                                                                            Page 352
                                       Page 19 of 25




        system equipment, or other required fire and life safety features in accordance
        with the CFC.

   9. Fire Protection System Installations and Modifications. Where compliance
      with this chapter requires the installation, extension, relocation, or modification of
      an automatic sprinkler system, fire detection system, or other required fire
      protection system, such work shall comply with the applicable CFC, BFC,
      associated NFPA standards, and shall be completed under a Fire Department
      Construction Permit in accordance with CFC §105.6.2 and §105.6.7 prior to
      installation.

12.32.110075 Stormwater Requirements


Waste Enclosure requirements. The following requirements apply to
all waste enclosures:


Waste enclosure structures shall be covered and designed to prevent stormwater runoff
from contacting waste materials. The roof canopy should extend sufficiently outward in
all directions so that windblown rain will not enter the interior of the storage area. A
horizontal or sloped canopy measuring approximately one-half the height of the canopy
to the ground is recommended. The waste enclosure shall include walls or other
barriers designed to prevent rainfall, stormwater run-on, and stormwater runoff from
entering or leaving the enclosure, and to minimize the wind dispersal of litter. Berms,
curbs, or other approved containment or diversion measures shall be incorporated, as
necessary, to prevent pollutant discharges to the municipal storm drain.


   1. Stormwater runoff from the enclosure roof must also drain away from the
        enclosure towards landscaping and/or stormwater treatment areas.



                                                                                   Page 353
                                       Page 20 of 25




   2. Waste enclosure floors shall be constructed of concrete and designed to prevent
       the discharge of runoff, wash water, or other liquids to the municipal storm drain.
       Discharges to the municipal storm drain system are prohibited. Floor drains,
       where permitted, shall discharge to the sanitary sewer, subject to approval by the
       applicable sanitary sewer agency.


   3. Waste enclosures shall be removed from public right-of-way and block view of
       waste receptacles from public right-of-way.


   4. No storm drains shall be located within the enclosure or in a location where
       stormwater could flow into or through the enclosure. The surrounding area shall
       be graded to prevent stormwater run-on. Grease interceptors, grease
       receptacles, and used cooking oil storage containers shall not be located within
       the trash enclosure unless specifically designed and permitted for such use. Any
       grease storage shall be covered, leak-proof, protected from stormwater run-on,
       and designed to prevent spills or discharges to the municipal storm drain.

12.32.180120 Putrescible waste--Procedure for management--Vermin infestation
               control--Prima facie presumption of violation.




                                                                                  Page 357
                                         Page 24 of 25




A. Any person possessing any premises wherein putrescible waste is produced,
handled, stored or allowed to accumulate shall manage such putrescible waste in such
a manner as to preclude the breeding of flies or other vermin therein.

B. No person in control of putrescible waste shall knowingly allow or permit the same
to serve as a breeding medium for flies or other vermin. Upon knowledge of such
infestation, or after receiving written notice from the manager of environmental health,
said person shall at once proceed and continue in good faith to destroy the flies, larvae
or pupae thereof by poisoning, trapping, removal of the material to a disposal site which
has been approved by the City, or by any other effective means.

C. In any prosecution charging violation of this chapter, a prima facie presumption of
the violation of the provisions of this section shall exist upon proof by the chief of
environmental health that an analysis of putrescible organic material controlled by any
person charged shows that such material contains living larvae or pupae of domestic
flies. (Ord. 6319-NS § 2 (part), 1996)

                                                                       October 27, 2026


TO:                    Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council

FROM:                  Councilmember Rashi Kesarwani (Author), Mayor Adena Ishii
                       (Co-Sponsor), Councilmember Terry Taplin (Co-Sponsor), and
                       Councilmember Ben Bartlett (Co-Sponsor)

SUBJECT:               Amendment to Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter
                       7.18 to Explicitly Require Competitive Procurement for Services
                       to Promote Accountability and Transparency and Refer
                       Development of Regulations to City Manager


RECOMMENDATION
Adopt an ordinance amending Berkeley Municipal Code (BMC) Chapter 7.18,
Expenditure Limitations, to require procurement through competitive solicitation for all
city contracts for professional services and other services greater than $100,000.

Further, for the City Attorney’s Office (CAO), require development of an Outside
Council Selection Protocol whereby the CAO develops an annual report to Council for
its pre-qualified list of outside attorneys and law firms based on respondents to the
office’s ongoing Request for Qualifications process. When outside counsel is required,
senior staff in the CAO would choose from pre-qualified attorneys/firms and identify
the best candidate based on expertise, quality of work, and cost. This recommendation
would allow for a competitive process using the pre-qualified list, thus accommodating
the CAO’s need to quickly engage outside counsel while preserving best procurement
practices. Additionally, request the CAO report to Council on legal services contracts
and amendments to City Council quarterly to increase transparency of spending on
legal services contracts.

Refer to the City Manager to promulgate any further regulations that may be needed
related to the requirement for competitive solicitation except for emergencies and when
market research justifies the business case for a sole-source procurement, in
alignment with the existing purchasing manual. Further, refer to the CAO to develop
legal services regulations to implement the competitive solicitation process for outside
counsel contracts and define circumstances where a sole-source procurement is
justified by emergencies, market research, conflicts of interest, or other considerations.

     Establishing annual reporting to Council on legal services contracts and amendments
     B.M.C. Section 7.18.010(A) Expenditures pursuant to Charter Article XI, Sections 67

Except as otherwise provided in this Title, expenditures pursuant to Article XI, Sections 67 and
67.5 of the Charter of the City of Berkeley, for which exceed the initial amount exceeds of
$1050,000, inclusive only of professional services, other services, supplies, equipment, or
materials (excluding leases and real estate agreements), shall require Council approval and

to Article XI, Section 67.4. The requirement specified in Article XI, Section 67 of the Charter to
select the “lowest responsible bidder” only for supplies, equipment, or materials contracts
remains. Professional services and other services contracts shall be based on demonstrated
competence and qualifications for the types of services to be performed, at fair and reasonable
prices to the City. This requirement for professional and other services contracts to be selected
via competitive procurement applies to all Charter Officers. Pursuant to Article XVI Section
113, the City Attorney retains the authority to enter into contracts without Council approval
after competitive procurement of professional services, other services, supplies, equipment or
